Universally attributed to Dōgen Zenji across quote databases (AZQuotes, Goodreads, etc.), but no specific chapter or fascicle of the Shobogenzo has been confirmed as the source in any search result found. The more literal and widely cited Dōgen translation is 'To let the self be awakened by all things is enlightenment' (appearing in multiple Shobogenzo editions). 'Enlightenment is intimacy with all things' reads as an interpretive paraphrase or secondary synthesis rather than a direct translation. The Shobogenzo (1231–1253) is the canonical primary source for Dōgen, but this exact phrasing cannot be pinned to a specific fascicle without further scholarly verification. Plausible but unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: I Am That: Talks with Sri Nisargadatta Maharaj, compiled by Maurice Frydman, 1973

And between the two my life flows.') is a minor paraphrase of the same passage. Also cited by Sharon Salzberg in 'Lovingkindness.' William Gladstone is cited in 'The Forbes Book of Business Quotations' (1997) and in 'The National Elementary School Principal' (Vol. 28, 1948) with a very similar phrasing. An even earlier origin attributed to William Ellery Channing (1780–1842) circulates but is unverified. No primary Hendrix source (interview, recording, written statement) has ever been established. Misattribution to Hendrix is well-documented.

Quote Investigator (quoteinvestigator.com/2020/05/13/make-friends/) investigated this thoroughly and concluded: 'based on current evidence this anecdote is apocryphal.' The saying has been attributed to Abraham Lincoln (via a post-mortem Civil War anecdote), Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund (d. 1437), and Mark Twain — all attributions appearing long after each figure's death. An 1867 New Orleans newspaper attributed a similar saying to Sigismund; the Lincoln anecdote form emerged by the 1940s. An 1858 Wisconsin newspaper cited the concept in relation to Cardinal Richelieu. An 1885 Vermont newspaper printed a similar line with no attribution. No primary Lincoln source (speech, letter, diary) has ever been found. The attribution to Lincoln is not credible.

No fabricated citation offered.

results.earliest_print_source: The Story of Philosophy, Will Durant, Simon & Schuster, 1926
results.notes: The pre-flag is correct and this is one of the best-documented misattributions in circulation. The sentence is Will Durant's own summarizing gloss on the Nicomachean Ethics (roughly 1103a-b, on virtue as hexis acquired by habituation), written in The Story of Philosophy (1926). Aristotle never wrote it; Durant's line is set immediately after his paraphrase of Aristotle and the quotation marks migrated over time. Wikiquote lists it under Aristotle's misattributed section. Recommend crediting Durant and, if the Aristotelian idea is wanted, citing Nicomachean Ethics directly instead.
results.suggested_reattribution: Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy (1926), paraphrasing Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics

results.earliest_print_source: John M. Culkin, "A Schoolman's Guide to Marshall McLuhan," Saturday Review, 18 March 1967
results.notes: The attribution as recorded in this record is already correct, which is unusual and worth preserving. Culkin wrote "We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us" while summarizing McLuhan's argument; McLuhan himself did not write the sentence in this form. Two cautions: (a) the corpus text "thereafter our tools shape us" is a later smoothing of Culkin's wording — consider restoring the original; (b) the line is often confused with Churchill's "We shape our buildings; thereafter they shape us" (House of Commons, 28 October 1943), which is a genuinely separate quotation and a likely source of the "thereafter" construction.

The creative mind plays with the objects it loves." The corpus text truncates "acting from inner necessity," which changes the emphasis somewhat — restoring the full sentence would be more faithful. Very widely and consistently attributed to Maslow, and entirely consistent with his writing on creativeness in Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) and The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (1971), where he discusses spontaneity and play in primary creativity. But I cannot place this exact eight-word sentence in either book or in any paper, and short aphoristic sentences of this shape are frequently condensations made by later writers rather than the author's own line. Honest verdict: probably Maslow-derived, source unconfirmed.

Lynch also used the formulation in talks about consciousness and Transcendental Meditation, and has framed it as echoing an Upanishadic idea rather than as his own invention — so "Lynch" is right as the popularizer but may not be right as the originator. Plausibly genuine, unsourced.

This aphorism's compressed, modern-English epigram form is unlike any authentic ghazal line. I did not attempt to name which Ladinsky volume it appears in, since I am not certain.

One of the most widely circulated Watts lines, and the work/play inversion is a genuine and central Watts theme rather than an internet invention. The idea (that life has no destination beyond the present moment) is thoroughly Watts, but this exact compressed sentence I cannot place in his books or in the lecture material I know. Short aphorisms in this shape are frequently distilled by others out of longer Watts passages and then quoted as if verbatim. Treat the wording as unverified even though the thought is his.

Strongly suspect. The vocabulary is wrong for Watts: 'degree of productivity' and 'presence' as a self-help metric belong to 2010s wellness writing, not to a mid-century writer whose target was the Protestant work ethic in quite different terms. I know of no occurrence in his published work, and this reads like an internet aphorism given a Watts byline for authority. I cannot name the actual author, so I have not proposed a reattribution — but I would not promote this as Watts.

Sounds authentically Watts and fits the argument of The Wisdom of Insecurity (1951), which is his sustained treatment of anxiety — that is the likeliest home for it. This formulation is classically Meister Eckhart's ('the soul is not in the body; the body is in the soul'), and the underlying doctrine is Plotinian — the Enneads argue expressly that the body is in the soul rather than the soul in the body. Watts read and quoted Eckhart constantly, so he may well have said this in a lecture, but he would have been relaying it, not coining it. Attributing it to Watts as author is likely wrong. My confidence in Eckhart as the formulator is moderate rather than high, hence the hedge.

Genuine Thich Nhat Hanh in substance and voice — attention as the most precious gift, and the blooming-flower image for those we attend to, are both signature formulations he used across many books and talks. The pairing appears in his Parallax Press volumes (How to Love is the collection most often cited for it), but he reworked these lines repeatedly and I cannot fix a first appearance, so I have left the print source null rather than guess a book.

Gandhi is a misattribution magnet, so I weighted this cautiously. Unlike most 'Gandhi' internet quotes, this one has a long and stable pre-internet circulation with consistent wording and is generally accepted as his, plausibly from a 1930s speech or writing collected in the Collected Works. But I cannot place it in a specific text or date, and I cannot rule out that it is a paraphrase tightened by a later editor. Attribution likely correct; evidence short of the promotion bar.

results.earliest_print_source: Walden; or, Life in the Woods, Henry David Thoreau, 1854, ch. 2 ("Where I Lived, and What I Lived For")
results.notes: Both fragments are genuine and come from the same famous passage in Walden ch. 2, but the ellipsis compresses several sentences. Thoreau's text runs: 'Our life is frittered away by detail... Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity! I say, let your affairs be as two or three... Simplify, simplify.' The condensation is faithful in sense but is not a contiguous quotation; if the corpus wants an exact citation, either restore the full passage or quote 'Simplify, simplify' on its own.

results.earliest_print_source: Meditations in Wall Street, Henry Stanley Haskins, 1940
results.notes: The first sentence is a well-documented misattribution. Quote Investigator traced 'What lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us' to Henry Stanley Haskins's anonymously published Meditations in Wall Street (1940); it is usually pinned on Emerson, sometimes on Thoreau or Oliver Wendell Holmes, and appears in the Misattributed section of Emerson's Wikiquote page. The second sentence ('And when you bring what is within out into the world, miracles happen') is a later accretion with no source at all — it is not in Haskins and not in Thoreau. The author field's hedge, 'Transcendentalist insight inspired by Henry David Thoreau,' is an invented byline; nothing here is Thoreau's. Recommend rejecting rather than reattributing, since the composite sentence as quoted matches no single source.
results.suggested_reattribution: Henry Stanley Haskins (first sentence only; second sentence has no known source)

results.earliest_print_source: Plato, Apology 38a (c. 399–390 BCE)
results.notes: Socrates' words as reported by Plato at his trial, Apology 38a: 'ho de anexetastos bios ou biotos anthropoi' — the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being. Standard, uncontested, and the single best-sourced Socrates quotation. Strictly speaking it is Plato's rendering of Socrates, who left no writings, but the attribution convention is universal.

This exact English sentence is a modern aphorism, not a translation of anything in Plato or Xenophon. The underlying idea is genuinely Socratic — the paradox 'no one errs willingly' (oudeis hekon hamartanei), argued in Protagoras 345d-e and developed in Meno and Gorgias, that wrongdoing is a form of ignorance rather than deliberate choice. But the compressed one-liner phrasing is contemporary and I cannot place who first put it this way. Defensible as a paraphrase clearly labeled as such; not defensible as a Socrates quotation.

results.earliest_print_source: Meditations, Marcus Aurelius, Book 2.11; this English wording from Gregory Hays's translation (Modern Library, 2002)
results.notes: Genuine, from Meditations 2.11. The crisp modern phrasing is specifically Gregory Hays's 2002 translation; older translations render it very differently (Long: 'Since it is possible that thou mayest depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly'). Worth crediting the translator if the corpus surfaces translation credits.

Consistently attributed to Shunryu Suzuki and, to my recollection, drawn from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind (Weatherhill, 1970), where the theme that practice is not preparation for a later attainment is central. I cannot confirm the chapter or page from memory, and the two sentences may be a condensation of a longer passage rather than a contiguous quotation, so I am leaving the print source null rather than asserting a locus I cannot check. The attribution itself is unlikely to be wrong; the citation is what is missing.

One of the most persistent Churchill misattributions. The International Churchill Society lists it among quotes falsely attributed to him: it appears nowhere in his speeches, books, or recorded remarks, and Churchill's own Wikiquote page files it under Misattributed. Variants of the underlying saying ('success is never final and failure never fatal') circulated in American motivational, business, and sportswriting from roughly the late 1930s onward, with no consistent author; the 'courage to continue' clause appears to be a later addition. I cannot identify a genuine originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution. Should not go live under Churchill's name.

Widely circulated as Picasso, almost always without any citation, and I know of no primary source — no interview, letter, or recorded remark. Picasso is a moderate misattribution magnet for epigrams about art and time. The line's idiom feels like late-20th-century American self-help/productivity writing rather than a translation from Picasso's French or Spanish, which further weakens the attribution. Honest answer: origin unknown, Picasso unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: De Brevitate Vitae (On the Shortness of Life), Seneca, c. 49 CE, ch. 14; this English wording from C. D. N. Costa's translation (Penguin, 1997)
results.notes: Genuine and correctly transcribed. This is the opening of De Brevitate Vitae 14, Seneca's argument that the philosopher annexes all past ages to his own lifetime. The English is C. D. N. Costa's Penguin translation, whose distinctive phrasing ('they annex every age to theirs', 'in loftiness of mind to pass beyond the narrow confines of human weakness') matches this text closely. Note the corpus context field says 'Ancient Greek' — Seneca was Roman and wrote in Latin.

results.earliest_print_source: Pro Plancio, Cicero, 54 BCE, §80
results.notes: Genuine Cicero, from the defense speech Pro Plancio: 'haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima, sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum' — this is the one virtue that is not only greatest but the parent of all the rest, said of gratitude. The English is the standard rendering found in quotation dictionaries. Section number 80 is from memory. Note the corpus context field says 'Ancient Greek'; Cicero was Roman.

The sentiment is squarely Ciceronian and matches the central argument of De Officiis Book III — that nothing dishonorable can genuinely be expedient, and that apparent utility gained through wrongdoing is not utility at all. But I cannot pin this English sentence to a specific passage, and I am not confident it renders a single Latin line rather than summarizing the argument. Plausible but uncited; do not promote without a checked locus in De Officiis. Corpus context field again wrongly lists Cicero as Greek.

I know of no such sentence anywhere in the Platonic corpus, and the 'an hour of X versus a year of Y' construction is a modern rhetorical shape, not a Greek one. It is sometimes defended as a gloss on Republic 536e-537a, where Socrates says children should be taught through play rather than compulsion — but that passage is about pedagogy, not about reading character, so the gloss does not hold. Plato is a heavy misattribution magnet for aphorisms of this kind. No genuine originator identifiable.

A modern condensation rather than a translation. The idea is authentically Epictetan and comes from Encheiridion 46, where he says not to call yourself a philosopher or talk about your principles among laymen, but to act on them — with the image of sheep that do not bring up grass to show the shepherd how much they ate, but produce wool and milk instead. No standard translation (Long, Higginson, Oldfather, Hard) contains this two-sentence English form; it reads like the loose contemporary paraphrase tradition around Epictetus. Safe to use if labeled a paraphrase of Encheiridion 46; not safe as a direct quotation.

results.earliest_print_source: Encheiridion (The Manual), Epictetus, c. 125 CE, §5
results.notes: The locus is certain: Encheiridion 5, the most quoted line in the whole handbook. Standard translations run 'Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things' (Long) or 'It is not events that disturb people, it is their judgements concerning them' (Hard). The wording here is a loose modern rendering rather than any established translation, so the attribution is solid while the exact phrasing is editorial. Consider aligning the text with a named translation.

results.earliest_print_source: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Seneca, Letter 13.4 (c. 65 CE)
results.notes: Genuine, from Letter 13, 'On Groundless Fears'. Gummere's Loeb translation reads: 'There are more things likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.' The quoted form drops 'often', which slightly strengthens the claim but does not distort it. Well documented and correctly attributed.

results.earliest_print_source: Meditations, Marcus Aurelius, Book 11.18 (c. 170–180 CE)
results.notes: Genuine, from the long passage in Meditations 11.18 on how to respond to people who wrong you, which closes on the claim that gentleness or kindness cannot be defeated when it is sincere — Hays renders it 'Kindness is invincible, provided it's sincere'. Translations split between 'gentleness' and 'kindness', so the three-word form here is a compression of a conditional sentence: Marcus qualifies it with 'if it be genuine'. Attribution is sound; the aphoristic trimming drops that qualifier.

results.earliest_print_source: De Tranquillitate Animi (On Tranquility of Mind), Seneca, c. 60 CE, §15
results.notes: Genuine Seneca, from the section of On Tranquility of Mind comparing Democritus, who laughed at human folly, with Heraclitus, who wept over it — Seneca sides with Democritus and says it better befits a man to laugh at life than to lament it. The English matches the Basore Loeb rendering closely. Section 15 is from memory; the work and the argument are certain.

Two separate issues. First, the author name is misspelled — 'Epectitus' should be 'Epictetus'. Second, this is a modern paraphrase, not a translation. The thought corresponds to Encheiridion 20: it is not the man who reviles you who insults you but your own judgement that the thing is insulting, so when someone provokes you it is your own opinion that has provoked you. The word 'complicit' and the whole register belong to the contemporary loose-paraphrase tradition around Epictetus (Sharon Lebell's The Art of Living, 1995, popularized renderings of exactly this kind), not to Long, Oldfather, or Hard. Usable if labeled a paraphrase of Encheiridion 20.
results.suggested_reattribution: Epictetus (spelling correction only, not a change of author)

results.notes: Attributed to Epictetus consistently in English quotation dictionaries going back to the nineteenth century, and the theme is the backbone of Discourses Book IV.1 ('On Freedom'), where he argues that the free man is the one who lives as he wishes and is enslaved by his own desires if by nothing else. But I cannot match this sentence to a specific passage, and the aphorism is close enough to Seneca's 'nemo liber est qui corpori servit' (Letter 92) that the two may have cross-contaminated in the quotation tradition. Plausible and old, but uncited; do not promote without a checked locus.

results.earliest_print_source: Encheiridion (The Manual), Epictetus, c. 125 CE, §8
results.notes: Genuine, from Encheiridion 8, one of the best-known lines in the handbook: do not seek to have events happen as you wish, but wish them to happen as they do, and your life will go well. The phrasing here is a variant translation rather than the standard Long or Hard wording, but it renders the same sentence and the locus is not in doubt.

I cannot match this to any chreia in Diogenes Laertius Book VI, which is the main source for sayings of Diogenes of Sinope, nor to any other ancient collection I know. The sentiment — that an insult disgraces the person who delivers it rather than its target — is a commonplace across ancient moral philosophy (compare Seneca's De Constantia Sapientis and Epictetus, Encheiridion 20), which makes a confident attribution to any one figure unsafe. Two further problems: 'infers' is almost certainly a corruption of 'offers' or 'utters', and the corpus context field labels Diogenes a Stoic when he was the founding Cynic. No true originator identifiable.

results.earliest_print_source: Vatican Sayings (Sententiae Vaticanae) 52, Epicurus (collection preserved in a Vatican Greek manuscript, first published 1888)
results.notes: Genuine Epicurus, Vatican Sayings 52 — commonly translated 'Friendship dances around the world, announcing to each of us that we must awaken to happiness' or 'bidding us all to awaken to the recognition of blessedness'. The wording here is a standard variant translation. One correction needed: the author is spelled 'Epicurius' in the input; it should be 'Epicurus'. The context field labels him Epicurean and Greek, which is right.
results.suggested_reattribution: Epicurus (spelling correction only, not a change of author)

results.notes: Consistently attributed to Schopenhauer and, to my recollection, drawn from the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life in Parerga und Paralipomena (1851), whose argument that what a man is in himself contributes far more to his happiness than what he has or how he is regarded matches this line exactly. I cannot confirm the chapter or the translator from memory, and the crisp English balance of 'difficult... impossible' may be a translator's or anthologist's polish rather than a literal rendering, so I am leaving the print source null. Attribution likely correct, citation unconfirmed.

Attributed to Schopenhauer with unusual consistency, largely because Erwin Schrodinger quoted it in his own work and gave it wide currency in scientific writing. I believe the attribution is genuine, but I cannot place the primary work — it is usually said to come from Schopenhauer's manuscript remains (Nachlass) rather than from a published book, which is exactly the kind of claim that gets repeated without checking. Also frequently seen in a shorter form ('The task is not to see what no one has yet seen, but to think what nobody has yet thought about what everybody sees'). Sound enough to keep, not sound enough to present as sourced.

results.earliest_print_source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. II, Ch. 31 ('On Genius'), Arthur Schopenhauer, 1844
results.notes: Genuine Schopenhauer. The German original runs roughly 'Das Talent gleicht dem Schuetzen, der ein Ziel trifft, welches die Uebrigen nicht erreichen koennen; das Genie dem, der eines trifft, bis zu welchem sie nicht einmal zu sehen vermoegen' — from the supplementary volume of Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (1844), chapter on genius. The English wording here is the standard condensed rendering rather than a literal translation of Payne or Haldane/Kemp, so the sense is Schopenhauer's but the phrasing is a popular paraphrase. Attribution itself is not in doubt.

Lennon is the weakest of the three candidate attributions. The saying is far more commonly credited to Yoko Ono, and it drifted onto Lennon posthumously the way many Ono lines did. A closely parallel and earlier documented line belongs to Dom Helder Camara — 'When we are dreaming alone it is only a dream. When we are dreaming with others, it is the beginning of reality' — from The Desert Is Fertile (1974). I cannot confirm from memory whether Ono's version predates or derives from Camara's, so I am not asserting a print source. What I am confident about is that the John Lennon attribution has no support I know of.

Consistently and exclusively attributed to Ram Dass, with no competing claimant I am aware of, and entirely idiomatic of his teaching voice. Like much of his circulating material it appears to come from recorded talks and satsang transcripts rather than a book I can name, so I cannot give a print citation. Attribution plausible-to-likely; source unlocated.

The famous case of an unlocatable attribution. The Institute for Intercultural Studies, which Mead herself founded, stated that it could not locate the quotation in her published writing, while noting the sentiment is consistent with her views and may come from an interview or informal remark. No primary source has ever been produced despite decades of searching. Author is plausible; documentation is absent.

Circulates as Merton, usually in the form 'A man who fails well is greater than one who succeeds badly.' The thought is congruent with Merton's writing on failure and false success, and I know of no rival attribution, but I cannot place it in a specific book — I would be guessing between No Man Is an Island, The Sign of Jonas, and the essay collections, so I am naming none of them.

Consistently attributed to Merton and characteristic of his writing on dialogue and mutual truth. I do not have a reliable memory of which volume it comes from — Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander is my hunch but not a knowledge claim, so I am leaving the print source null rather than risk laundering a guess into a citation.

Genuine Merton in substance and phrasing; the interdependence-as-ground-of-compassion theme runs through his late Buddhist-facing work, and the wording matches his prose closely enough that I doubt it is a paraphrase. Commonly cited to Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander (1966), and sometimes to the Asian journal material, but I cannot resolve between them from memory, so no print source asserted.

results.earliest_print_source: No Man Is an Island, Thomas Merton, 1955
results.notes: One of the best-documented Merton passages. The standard citation in scholarly and popular references alike is No Man Is an Island (Harcourt, Brace, 1955), from the opening material on love, and the quoted text matches Merton's published wording. I am confident in book and year from memory of the standard reference; I have not verified a page number and am not supplying one.

results.earliest_print_source: Auguries of Innocence, William Blake, written c. 1803, first published 1863 in Gilchrist's Life of William Blake
results.notes: The opening quatrain of Auguries of Innocence, from the Pickering Manuscript. Attribution is beyond dispute. Two transcription defects in the corpus text should be fixed before publication: 'infintiy' is a typo for 'infinity', and Blake's text reads 'a Wild Flower' (two words) not 'a wildflower'. Blake's line breaks are four lines, not two; the canonical text is 'To see a World in a Grain of Sand / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower, / Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand / And Eternity in an hour.'

The author is right but the wording is a modern compression. Churchill's documented line, from a wartime minute, runs: 'The maxim Nothing avails but perfection may be spelt shorter — Paralysis.' That is the genuine article; 'Perfectionism spells paralysis' is a paraphrase that circulates in business and productivity writing. I recall the minute being reproduced in the appendices of The Second World War but cannot pin the volume, so no print source asserted. Also note the author field misspells the name — it should be 'Winston Churchill', not 'Churchil'. Churchill is a known misattribution magnet, but here the underlying attribution is sound; only the phrasing is secondhand.

results.earliest_print_source: Discourses, Book I, Ch. 2, Epictetus (recorded by Arrian, c. 108 CE)
results.notes: This tracks a real passage in Discourses I.2, where Epictetus argues from the athlete's example that we do not abandon a discipline out of despair of ever being the best at it. Translations vary considerably and the corpus wording matches no standard translation I know (Long, Oldfather, Hard), so treat it as a loose modern rendering rather than a quotation. Confidence is in the attribution to Epictetus, which I hold as strong; the exact English is not his translator's. Also note the author field misspells the name — it should be 'Epictetus', not 'Epectitus'.

Very widely circulated as Warhol, almost always without a citation. I cannot place it in The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (1975), POPism (1980), or the published diaries, which is where a line this quotable would be expected to sit. The register also reads more like contemporary creative-advice writing than Warhol's clipped, deadpan speech. I do not have evidence identifying a true author, so I am not proposing a reattribution — but the attribution should be treated as unsupported.

results.earliest_print_source: 'The Guts of a New Machine', Rob Walker, The New York Times Magazine, 30 November 2003
results.notes: Jobs said this to Rob Walker in the New York Times Magazine piece on the iPod. The fuller passage runs 'Most people make the mistake of thinking design is what it looks like... That's not what we think design is. It's not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.' The condensed form quoted here is faithful to the sense and is the version that entered general circulation.

Consistently attributed to Jobs and consistent with his stated posture on killing products quickly. My recollection places it in an interview rather than a speech — a Fortune profile from the late 2000s is my impression — but I cannot fix the outlet or date with enough confidence to name one, so the print source stays null. No competing attribution known.

results.earliest_print_source: Apple Worldwide Developers Conference closing Q&A, Steve Jobs, May 1997
results.notes: From the well-known WWDC 1997 fireside/Q&A session Jobs held shortly after returning to Apple — the same session that produced the 'start with the customer experience and work backwards to the technology' answer. The passage is widely reproduced from the recording and is also quoted in Isaacson's biography. I am confident in the venue and year; the exact date within the conference I have not verified.

results.earliest_print_source: Stanford University Commencement Address, Steve Jobs, 12 June 2005
results.notes: Verbatim from the third story ('about death' — actually this passage closes the second story, on love and loss) of the Stanford commencement address. Full text is published by Stanford and the video is a matter of record. Attribution and wording both solid.

Ubiquitous as a Disney quotation, including in Disney-affiliated merchandise and park signage, but I know of no primary source — no interview, memo, speech, or contemporaneous account. Late-appearing attributions of this kind to Disney are common. The sentiment is unobjectionable and no rival author is known to me, so I am not calling it apocryphal, but it should not clear a verification bar.

Long and consistently attributed to Bell, and it appears in older quotation compendia rather than only in modern internet collections, which is a point in its favour — many bogus attributions have no pre-web trail at all. I cannot name the speech, letter, or article it came from, so no print source is asserted. Attribution likely; documentation unlocated.

Marysarah Quinn is a real person — a book designer and creative director in trade publishing — and the obscurity of the name is mildly reassuring, since invented attributions gravitate toward famous names rather than away from them. But I cannot place this line in anything she wrote or is recorded as saying. My impression is that it entered circulation via an anthology or an essay quoting her in conversation, which I cannot confirm. Honest answer: I don't know.

'Ian Wallace' here is not an author but a fictional character — the line is spoken by Ian Wallace (played by Oliver James) in the 2003 film What a Girl Wants, and the credit therefore belongs to the screenwriters, Jenny Bicks and Elizabeth Chandler, working from the play The Reluctant Debutante. The quote is also frequently and wrongly attributed to Dr. Seuss, which is a separate and clearly false attribution. Recommend either recrediting to the film or dropping the item, since attributing dialogue to a character as if he were a person is misleading.
results.suggested_reattribution: Jenny Bicks and Elizabeth Chandler, screenwriters — spoken by the character Ian Wallace in the film What a Girl Wants (2003)

results.notes: Firmly associated with Ella Baker and adopted as the motto of the Ella Baker Center for Human Rights, which is meaningful secondary support. One caveat worth recording: Baker is understood to have used the line as an existing adage rather than coined it, so 'Ella Baker said this' is well supported while 'Ella Baker originated this' may not be. I cannot name the speech or interview in which she used it.

results.earliest_print_source: Upstream: Selected Essays, Mary Oliver, 2016
results.notes: From Oliver's essay collection Upstream, where it appears in her discussion of attention as the ground of a devoted life. The line is quoted from that book widely and correctly. I am confident in book and year; page unverified.

Genuine Thich Nhat Hanh in substance — this is his well-known verse on no-birth and no-death, which he wrote for use at funerals and which the Plum Village community recites. It is commonly cited to No Death, No Fear (2002), and I believe it appears there, but the wording here differs from the version I recall ('This body is not me. I am not caught in this body. I am life without boundaries. I have never been born and I have never died...'), so this looks like a variant translation or an abridgement. Attribution to Thich Nhat Hanh is strong; the specific text and its source edition are not confirmed, hence no print citation.

Idiomatic of Mooji and consonant with his 'be nothing, know nothing, have nothing' teaching, and I know of no competing attribution. But his material circulates almost entirely as satsang transcripts and social-media cards, and I cannot place this aphorism in a specific book or recorded talk. Plausible but undocumented in my knowledge.

Same situation as the companion Mooji item. The line reads as authentic Mooji and no rival author is known to me; my impression is that it belongs to the aphorism collections such as White Fire (2014), but that is an impression rather than a recollection I can stand behind, so no print source is given. Living teachers' quotations are hard to verify without a recording or a page reference, and I have neither.

Consistently attributed to Wei Wu Wei (pen name of Terence Gray, 1895-1986), the Irish writer on Advaita, Ch'an and Taoism. The line is stylistically and doctrinally characteristic of his aphoristic books of the 1960s, and I know of no competing attribution. I cannot place the exact volume or page from training knowledge - candidates are 'Ask the Awakened: The Negative Way' (1963) and 'All Else Is Bondage: Non-Volitional Living' (1964) - so I leave the print source null rather than guess. Author attribution strong; citation unlocated.

results.earliest_print_source: Ask the Awakened: The Negative Way, Wei Wu Wei, 1963
results.notes: This is Wei Wu Wei's single most-quoted line and is routinely cited to 'Ask the Awakened: The Negative Way' (1963), where it appears in the opening/epigraph material. My recollection of that book association is firm but I cannot confirm the page, so a human should spot-check the citation before it is treated as primary-source verified. No competing attribution exists; the phrasing ('and there isn't one') is distinctively his.

results.earliest_print_source: Speech at the launch of Mindset Network, University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, 16 July 2003
results.notes: Genuine Mandela. Delivered at the 2003 Mindset Network launch in Johannesburg; the Nelson Mandela Foundation has confirmed this speech as the source, and it is the standard citation on Wikiquote. Wording in circulation is stable and matches the delivered text.

results.earliest_print_source: Ten Principles for Good Design (principle 10), Dieter Rams, formulated late 1970s-1980s
results.notes: This is verbatim the tenth of Rams's 'Ten Principles for Good Design' ('Good design is as little design as possible'), including the gloss 'Less, but better - because it concentrates on the essential aspects... Back to purity, back to simplicity.' The principles are documented by Vitsoe and reproduced in the Rams literature (e.g. 'Weniger, aber besser / Less but Better', 1995). Attribution is not in doubt.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Design by Vitsoe' (speech, New York, 1976), Dieter Rams
results.notes: Well-known Rams line, consistently attributed to his 1976 'Design by Vitsoe' address given at Jack Lenor Larsen's New York showroom, which is the usual source given in the Rams literature. My recollection of that specific speech is good but not certain enough to call primary-source verified; the author attribution itself is not in doubt.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Design by Vitsoe' (speech, New York, 1976), Dieter Rams
results.notes: Attributed to Rams and, in my recollection, drawn from the same 1976 'Design by Vitsoe' address as q_0142 - the two passages are frequently quoted together. Wording in circulation varies slightly (translations from the German differ), which is why I stop short of verified. No competing attribution.

results.earliest_print_source: A Study in Scarlet, Arthur Conan Doyle, 1887
results.notes: Spoken by Sherlock Holmes in 'A Study in Scarlet' (1887); the credit line in the corpus ('Sherlock Holmes, via Conan Doyle') correctly separates character from author. I am confident of the novel; I cannot pin the chapter from memory. Note that it is a fictional character's line, not Doyle speaking in his own voice.

Very widely and consistently attributed to Gandhi, and consonant with his writing on ahimsa, but I cannot place it in a specific issue of Young India, Harijan, or the Collected Works from training knowledge. Gandhi is a major misattribution magnet, so I hold this below the promotion bar until someone can point to a dated original. Attribution plausible and uncontested; citation unlocated.

Genuinely Mother Teresa's sentiment, expressed many times in slightly different words; the most commonly documented form is 'We can do no great things, only small things with great love.' The wording here is a widespread variant that appears in the posthumous compilations (e.g. 'A Simple Path', 1995; 'The Joy in Loving'). Because she repeated the thought in varying phrasings and I cannot fix this exact sentence to a dated text, I keep it just below the bar.

The book is real - Chris Anderson (head of TED), 'Infectious Generosity: The Ultimate Idea Worth Spreading' (2024) - and the passage's framework (emotion, creativity, courage, collaboration, amplification as multipliers of generosity) matches the book's actual argument. But it is recent and I cannot confirm this exact wording or locate the page from training knowledge, so the citation stands on the corpus's own claim rather than on independent evidence. Verifiable by anyone with the book; treat as unconfirmed until then.

results.earliest_print_source: The World According to Mister Rogers: Important Things to Remember, Fred Rogers, 2003
results.notes: Authentic Fred Rogers. He told the 'look for the helpers' story repeatedly - on Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, in interviews, and in print - and the Fred Rogers Center has affirmed it as genuinely his. It appears in the 2003 collection 'The World According to Mister Rogers,' which is the citation I recall, though the story predates that book in his broadcast work. Wording in circulation is stable.

This exact sentence has never been located in Jung's Collected Works, letters, or seminars despite very heavy circulation. The genuine Jungian source it paraphrases is 'Aion' (1951), CW 9ii, para. 126: 'When an inner situation is not made conscious, it appears outside as fate.' So the idea is authentically Jung's while the popular wording is a modern compression by an unknown hand. Recommend either replacing with the sourced Aion sentence or labeling this as a paraphrase. Not a misattribution to a different author, so no reattribution offered.

The book is real - Rick Rubin with Neil Strauss, 'The Creative Act: A Way of Being' (Penguin Press, 2023) - and this passage is entirely consistent with its content and voice; the book contains material on nature as teacher and on the artist's non-separateness. I cannot confirm the exact wording or locate the chapter from training knowledge, so the citation rests on the corpus's own claim. Easy for a human to verify against the book; until then, unconfirmed rather than doubted.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Where Do We Go from Here?', SCLC Presidential Address, Atlanta, 16 August 1967
results.notes: Authentic King. He used the formulation more than once - it appears in the 1967 SCLC presidential address 'Where Do We Go from Here?' and in adjacent sermons on love and nonviolence ('Loving Your Enemies'; the 1967 Christmas sermon on peace). Attribution is not in question; the specific occasion cited is the one I am most confident of.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter from Birmingham Jail, Martin Luther King, Jr., 16 April 1963
results.notes: Verbatim from the 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (16 April 1963), early in the letter where King answers the clergymen's charge that he is an outside agitator. The full run - 'cognizant of the interrelatedness... inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny' - matches the published text. As solid a provenance as this corpus will contain.

No French original in Voltaire's works corresponds to this line as far as I know, and it circulates almost exclusively in English aphorism collections and on quote sites without a citation. Voltaire is one of the strongest misattribution magnets in the corpus of freethought quotations (the fabricated 'I disapprove of what you say...' line being the classic case). The related genuine sentiment usually cited is Goethe's 'None are more hopelessly enslaved than those who falsely believe they are free,' which is a different quote. I have no defensible true origin, so no reattribution. Recommend rejection or a clear 'attributed to' hedge.

results.earliest_print_source: Speech in Selma, Alabama, 8 March 1965
results.notes: Authentic King, generally sourced to his remarks in Selma on 8 March 1965 (the day after Bloody Sunday), which is the citation carried on Wikiquote and in King anthologies. My confidence in the King attribution is high; my confidence in that exact date and occasion is good but not certain, which is why I stop short of verified.

results.earliest_print_source: Strength to Love, Martin Luther King, Jr., 1963 (sermon 'Loving Your Enemies')
results.notes: Authentic King, from the 'Loving Your Enemies' sermon collected in 'Strength to Love' (1963). One wording caution: King's published sentence ends 'plunged into the dark abyss of annihilation,' not 'the darkness of annihilation,' and the passage here is a condensation joining sentences separated in the original by the ellipsis. Recommend restoring the published wording. Attribution itself is beyond doubt.

results.earliest_print_source: 'I've Been to the Mountaintop', Mason Temple, Memphis, 3 April 1968
results.notes: King said this in his final speech, 'I've Been to the Mountaintop,' the night before his assassination: 'Only when it is dark enough can you see the stars.' Worth noting for the corpus that King was invoking an older aphorism, commonly credited to the historian Charles A. Beard and sometimes loosely to Emerson; King is the popularizer rather than the originator of the thought, but the utterance attributed to him is genuine.

I cannot locate this sentence in Wilde's plays, essays, letters, or the 'Phrases and Philosophies for the Use of the Young.' It reads like a compression of two documented Wilde lines: 'Life is far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it' (Lady Windermere's Fan, 1892; also in Vera) and 'We should treat all the trivial things of life seriously, and all the serious things of life with sincere and studied triviality.' Wilde attracts unsourced epigrams the way Twain attracts folksy ones. Also frequently confused with Niels Bohr's 'There are some things so serious you have to laugh at them.' No confident true origin, so no reattribution.

The pre-flag is correct. This appears in no Einstein primary source and is absent from Alice Calaprice's 'The Ultimate Quotable Einstein,' the standard scholarly filter; documented instances begin decades after Einstein's 1955 death, in late-twentieth-century business, advertising, and creativity literature. Quote investigators have pointed at a modern advertising/creativity author (I recall Joey Reiman being named) as an early user rather than Einstein, but my recollection of that trail is not firm enough to assert a reattribution, so I leave the field null. Recommend rejection or relabeling as anonymous.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter of condolence to the family of Michele Besso, 21 March 1955 (published in the Einstein-Besso correspondence; quoted in 'Einstein: The Human Side')
results.notes: Unlike most 'Einstein' aphorisms this one has a real root: writing to Michele Besso's family weeks before his own death, Einstein wrote that for believing physicists 'the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubborn persistent illusion.' The version in the corpus is a loose paraphrase - it pluralizes 'illusions' and drops the crucial framing 'for us believing physicists,' which changes the claim from a remark about physics to a metaphysical assertion. Attribution to Einstein is genuine; this wording is not his. Strongly recommend replacing with the accurate translation, after which it would merit verified status.

results.earliest_print_source: Martha: The Life and Work of Martha Graham, Agnes de Mille, 1991
results.notes: Authentically Agnes de Mille and consistently attributed to her; the passage is the well-known one whose elided middle reads 'The moment you know how, you begin to die a little.' It is usually cited to her Graham biography 'Martha: The Life and Work of Martha Graham' (1991), the same book that carries the famous Graham 'divine dissatisfaction' passage, and I believe that citation is right but cannot confirm the page. No competing attribution.

The idea is genuinely Rogers's, but this four-word form is not his wording. In 'On Becoming a Person' (1961), in the chapter 'This Is Me,' he writes 'what is most personal is most general.' The variant 'what is most personal is most universal' circulates widely and is sometimes attributed to Rogers directly, sometimes to later writers restating him. 'The personal is the universal' is a further compression by an unknown hand and may also be blending with the second-wave feminist slogan 'the personal is political' (Carol Hanisch, 1969). Recommend replacing with the sourced 1961 sentence.

results.earliest_print_source: Music at Night and Other Essays, Aldous Huxley, 1931 (essay 'The Rest Is Silence')
results.notes: Genuine Huxley, from 'Music at Night and Other Essays' (1931), in the essay 'The Rest Is Silence.' The sentence circulates verbatim and matches the published text. One of the reliably sourced quotations in this batch.

Alan Cohen is a real inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, A Deep Breath of Life, Wisdom of the Heart) and this line circulates consistently under his name on quote sites and in daily-inspiration compilations. I cannot place it in a specific book, chapter, or dated column from training knowledge, and Cohen's aphorisms are almost always recirculated without citation. The attribution is plausible and uncontested but unsourced.

Consistently attributed to Gandhi across collections, and the ocean/drops image is idiomatically consistent with his writing in Young India and Harijan. However, I cannot locate a primary source — no specific issue, speech, or volume of the Collected Works comes to mind, and I do not know whether this sits in the sourced or the unsourced section of Gandhi's Wikiquote page. Gandhi is a heavy misattribution magnet, so consistent repetition is not itself evidence. Honest verdict: plausibly genuine, unverified.

The pre-flag is correct. There is no Gandhi source for this; it does not appear in the Collected Works so far as I know, and it is generally listed among Gandhi's misattributed lines. The saying is far older than Gandhi: a closely matching maxim ('Study as if you were to live forever; live as if you were to die tomorrow') is traditionally ascribed to St. Edmund of Abingdon, the 13th-century Archbishop of Canterbury, and circulated in English proverb collections well before Gandhi's lifetime. The James Dean attribution is a separate later graft and is also unsupported. I am confident it is not Gandhi's; I am only moderately confident in the Edmund of Abingdon lineage, which is itself a tradition rather than a documented autograph.
results.suggested_reattribution: Traditional maxim long ascribed to St. Edmund of Abingdon (13th c.); not Gandhi

results.earliest_print_source: Statement to Christian Zervos, 'Conversation avec Picasso,' Cahiers d'Art, 1935
results.notes: This belongs to Picasso's well-known 1935 statement recorded by Christian Zervos and published in Cahiers d'Art, the same conversation that produced 'a picture is not thought out and settled beforehand.' The English rendering circulating today comes from the translation reprinted in Alfred H. Barr Jr.'s Picasso monograph and in Herschel B. Chipp's Theories of Modern Art (1968). I am confident about the 1935 Zervos conversation as the origin but have not pinned the exact page in the translated reprints, so I am holding just under the promotion bar rather than claiming primary verification.

Idiomatically very close to Watts's recurring theme that naming and classifying substitute for direct perception (developed at length in The Wisdom of Insecurity and The Book), but I cannot place this exact sentence in any Watts book or transcribed lecture. Watts's recorded talks are a large, loosely transcribed corpus, which makes attractive one-liners easy to attach to him without evidence. Plausible but unsourced.

The thought is authentically Jungian — it matches his insistence that the psyche is not contained inside the skull ('we are in the psyche' rather than the psyche being in us) and his late work on synchronicity and the unus mundus. But I cannot locate this exact sentence in the Collected Works, the letters, or Memories, Dreams, Reflections. Jung is frequently paraphrased into crisper English than he wrote, and this reads like such a condensation. Unsourced.

results.earliest_print_source: 'The Most Durable Power,' Martin Luther King Jr., The Christian Century, 1957 (from a sermon delivered at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery, November 1956)
results.notes: This is King's own language from the sermon/essay 'The Most Durable Power,' delivered at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church during the closing weeks of the Montgomery bus boycott and excerpted in The Christian Century in 1957; it is indexed in The Papers of Martin Luther King, Jr. and reprinted in A Testament of Hope. The wording here (durable power / creative force / exemplified in the life of our Christ / quest for peace and security) matches the published text. I am confident in the sermon and the Christian Century publication; I am not certain of the exact issue date, so treat the year rather than a day as the firm part of the citation.

results.earliest_print_source: 'What I Believe,' Albert Einstein, Forum and Century, vol. 84, 1930; collected in The World As I See It, 1931 (Mein Weltbild, 1934)
results.notes: Genuine Einstein, and unusually well documented for him. This is the closing passage of his credo essay 'What I Believe,' published in Forum and Century in 1930 and collected in The World As I See It. The long form quoted here matches the standard English translation, including 'as good as dead; his eyes are closed' and the concluding 'this knowledge, this feeling is at the center of true religiousness.' Truncated one-line versions circulate widely, but the full passage given here is faithful.

The pre-flag is correct. There is no Einstein source for this, in his published papers, essays, letters, or the standard quotation references. It reads as a design-industry aphorism of recent vintage, most likely a loose descendant of the genuine Einstein simplicity theme (see q_0180) that acquired his name for authority. I cannot identify a real originator, so 'apocryphal' rather than 'likely_misattributed' — I have no probable true author to offer, and inventing one would be worse than admitting that.

results.earliest_print_source: Roger Sessions, 'How a Difficult Composer Gets That Way,' The New York Times, January 8, 1950
results.notes: The idea is Einstein's; the epigram is not his wording. Einstein's documented statement is from the 1933 Herbert Spencer Lecture 'On the Method of Theoretical Physics': the supreme goal of all theory is to make the irreducible basic elements as simple and as few as possible without surrendering the adequate representation of a single datum of experience. The compact form entered print when the composer Roger Sessions reported it secondhand in the New York Times in 1950 — explicitly as a remark Einstein made 'in effect,' i.e. Sessions's own condensation. Everything since descends from that paraphrase. Genuine sentiment, secondhand phrasing; deliberately held below the promotion bar because the corpus would be presenting a paraphrase as Einstein's words.

results.earliest_print_source: Richard L. Evans's Quote Book, 1971 (crediting Carl W. Buehner)
results.notes: The pre-flag is right to hedge. Angelou did use versions of this in interviews and talks from the 1990s onward, so the attribution is not fabricated — but the aphorism predates her. The earliest known instance credits Carl W. Buehner: 'They may forget what you said, but they will never forget how you made them feel,' printed in Richard L. Evans's Quote Book (1971). Angelou's characteristic triad ('what you said / what you did / how you made them feel') is her expansion of an existing saying, and I cannot fix a first Angelou utterance or its exact wording. Safest handling: treat the wording as unverified and do not present it as an original Angelou line.

Definitely not Lincoln — nothing like it appears in the Collected Works, and the managerial idiom is anachronistic for the 1860s; it is a standard Lincoln graft. The Drucker attribution in the author field is the common replacement but is itself weakly evidenced: I cannot point to the book or article where Drucker wrote it. The best-documented neighbor is Alan Kay's 'The best way to predict the future is to invent it' (Xerox PARC, early 1970s), and Dennis Gabor's Inventing the Future (1963) argues that the future cannot be predicted but can be invented. The 'create it' variant floats between Drucker, Kay, Gabor, and Forrest Shaklee. Since I cannot say which is right, no reattribution.

Consistently and, as far as I know, uncontestedly attributed to the American essayist Agnes Repplier (1855-1950), and the epigrammatic balance is characteristic of her prose. It is usually cited to one of her essay collections — Compromises (1904) is the volume most often named — but I cannot confirm the volume or essay from memory, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing. Attribution is stable; the citation is not established.

Same situation as q_0166. Attributed to Alan Cohen wherever it appears and consistent with his register, but recirculated without citation and not placeable in a specific book or column from training knowledge. Uncontested but unsourced.

As with the other two Alan Cohen entries in this batch: plausible, uncontested, and unsourced. I cannot place it in a titled work, and Cohen's material circulates chiefly through daily-inspiration excerpts that drop citations.

Strongly Wattsian in both idea and vocabulary — 'aperture' is a word he genuinely used for the individual as the universe's point of self-awareness, and the thought parallels the documented passages in The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are (1966) about the universe peopling and looking at itself through our eyes. I cannot confirm this exact sentence in a printed Watts text, and much of the Watts material online comes from loosely transcribed lectures. Likely genuine in substance, wording unverified.

One of the most widely reproduced Watts lines, attributed to him with unusual consistency and squarely on the theme of The Wisdom of Insecurity (1951), which is the book most often cited for it. I cannot confirm the page or even the volume from memory, so I am not recording a print source. The stability of the attribution earns 'attributed,' but without a located passage it stays below the promotion bar.

No primary source. This is one of the modest-genius lines that accrete to Einstein, and I cannot trace it to a paper, letter, or documented interview. The genuine, well-sourced neighbor is his letter to Carl Seelig of 11 March 1952: 'I have no special talents. I am only passionately curious.' The 'stay with problems longer' phrasing looks like a later restatement of that sentiment rather than something Einstein wrote. Uncertain, and Einstein's misattribution record argues for caution.

No Einstein source exists for this; it is routinely listed among his misattributed quotations. The phrasing is late-20th/21st-century motivational English and has the shape of a slogan retrofitted with a famous name — it may owe something to popularized readings of adaptability in intelligence research, but I know of no real originator and will not guess one. Recommend it not be promoted under Einstein's name in any form.

results.earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Text, Chapter 21, Introduction (T-21.in.1), Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976
results.notes: Genuine and locatable. This is the opening of Chapter 21 of the ACIM Text ('Reason and Perception'), which begins 'Projection makes perception' and continues through 'Therefore, seek not to change the world, but choose to change your mind about the world.' The second sentence quoted here ('What you see reflects your thinking...') is from the same introductory passage. Wording matches the Foundation for Inner Peace edition. Note the source is a work, not a person — the corpus should credit A Course in Miracles rather than Helen Schucman personally, which matches the input.

The sentence matches ACIM's definition of the ego as the mind's belief in its own separation and autonomy, and it is quoted as ACIM in the secondary literature around the Course (Wapnick and others). I cannot pin the chapter and section, and ACIM circulates in multiple editions with different numbering, so I am not recording a citation I cannot place. Very likely genuine to the work; location unconfirmed.

Reads as authentic ACIM in cadence and doctrine (freedom of belief, and behavior as the witness to belief), and it is quoted as such, but I cannot locate the passage in the Text, Workbook, or Manual for Teachers from memory. Slightly lower confidence than q_0191 because I have less independent recall of this specific line. Genuine-looking but unlocated.

Extremely widely attributed to Helen Keller and not, to my knowledge, contested or reassigned to anyone else — but I cannot trace it to a book, essay, letter, or speech of hers. It is a staple of teamwork posters and fundraising copy, which is exactly the environment in which citations disappear. Plausible; unsourced.

results.earliest_print_source: Robert G. Ingersoll, lecture 'Abraham Lincoln,' 1883
results.notes: Not Lincoln. Nothing of the kind appears in the Collected Works, and the attribution is 20th-century. The near-certain origin is Robert G. Ingersoll's celebrated lecture on Lincoln (1883), which argues: 'Nothing discloses real character like the use of power... Most people can bear adversity; but if you wish to know what a man really is, give him power.' A statement made *about* Lincoln was over time converted into a statement *by* Lincoln — a common mechanism for this particular magnet. Confidence value reflects the weakness of the Lincoln attribution; my confidence in the Ingersoll origin is considerably higher.
results.suggested_reattribution: Robert G. Ingersoll, from his 1883 lecture on Abraham Lincoln

results.earliest_print_source: Toward a Psychology of Being, Abraham H. Maslow, 1962
results.notes: The thought is documented Maslow: Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) frames growth as a repeated choice, in the form 'one can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth,' with growth chosen over and over and fear overcome again and again. The wording quoted here ('You will either step forward in growth or you will step back into safety') is the popular circulating variant rather than the printed sentence I can attest to, and it is often given in the second person as if from a lecture. Substance verified in the 1962 book; exact wording is a variant, so it should be presented as Maslow's idea, ideally with the printed phrasing substituted.

results.earliest_print_source: Toward a Psychology of Being, Abraham H. Maslow, 1962
results.notes: This is Maslow's core safety-versus-growth dialectic, which he develops explicitly in Toward a Psychology of Being (1962), especially the 'Defense and Growth' material where he frames each moment as a choice between the delights/anxieties of safety and those of growth. The line is consistently attributed to that book across psychology literature and I recall it as Maslow's own phrasing rather than a paraphrase. I cannot confirm a page number from memory, so this is strong secondary rather than page-verified.

Abraham-Hicks material is channeled workshop transcript published by Esther and Jerry Hicks; individual passages circulate with a workshop city and date on the official site and in the Daily Quote mailings. The vocabulary and cadence here (the abundance 'flowing in many more avenues than dollars', 'delicious people', the recursive stacking of 'the abundance of...') is highly characteristic of the Abraham corpus, so authorship is plausible. But I cannot place this passage in a specific workshop, recording, or book, and transcript excerpts are routinely re-cut and paraphrased by quote sites. Attribution to the source is plausible; the exact wording is unverified.

Alan Cohen is a real and prolific inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, A Deep Breath of Life, Wisdom of the Heart, Enough Already), and this line is consistent with his aphoristic voice and his recurring 'the treasure is within you' theme. However, I cannot place it in a specific book, chapter, or newsletter. His one-liners circulate almost entirely through quote aggregators and his own daily-inspiration mailings, which leaves no verifiable print chain. Honest verdict: plausible author, no evidence.

This longer passage ('we are divinely created love machines', well-being depends on giving rather than receiving love) reads as genuine Alan Cohen prose rather than a quote-site fragment — the paragraph structure and the gentle contrarian turn are his. I have a weak recollection of this theme in his book-length work but cannot name the title or year with any confidence, and I will not guess one. Attribution plausible, source unlocated.

Consistent with Alan Cohen's writing on self-care and the helper's blind spot, and widely reproduced under his name. No specific book, article, or dated newsletter can be identified from my training knowledge, and no primary text is available to confirm the wording. Plausible but unevidenced.

Attributed to Alan Cohen across quote sites and thematically of a piece with q_0198 (greatness is internal, not imported). Note the transmitted text is ungrammatical — 'is turn your back' is missing 'to', which is a signature of quote-aggregator copying rather than a book text, and suggests the wording here has drifted from whatever the original was. No source located; no independent evidence for the attribution.

The 'watch what follows I AM' teaching is a shared commonplace of New Thought and metaphysical writing (Emmet Fox, Florence Scovel Shinn, Wayne Dyer, Joel Goldsmith and many others all state versions of it), so this particular phrasing is not distinctive enough for me to assign it to Alan Cohen on internal evidence. He may well have written it; the idea is not original to him. No source located.

This is a variant of the widely circulated 'Imagination is everything. It is the preview of life's coming attractions,' which is popularly attributed to Albert Einstein and has no basis in his writings — it is a well-known apocryphal Einstein line. The 'coming attractions' movie-trailer metaphor therefore has muddled provenance predating any Cohen usage, and the same sentence also floats attributed to Louise Hay and others. Alan Cohen may have used this phrasing, but the attribution chain is contaminated. Low confidence in the recorded author; I cannot identify who coined the movie-trailer formulation.

Gratitude-versus-complaint framing stated as a ratio; consistent with Alan Cohen's aphoristic style and widely reproduced under his name. No book, article, or dated source identifiable from training knowledge.

A reworking of the older idiom 'waiting for my ship to come in' (which is a proverbial commonplace, not anyone's coinage) and close in shape to several circulating variants such as 'Don't wait for your ship to come in — swim out to it' and 'your ship has already come in.' The specific inversion here is attributed to Alan Cohen on quote sites, but the idiom's ubiquity makes independent coinage likely in multiple mouths. No source located.

Reads like an instruction from a practice-oriented passage or daily-inspiration entry, which matches how most Alan Cohen quotations enter circulation. Plausibly his; no specific book, chapter, or dated mailing identifiable, and no independent corroboration of the attribution.

The construction ('radiate wholeness, a rare delicacy in a world of hungry hearts') is more crafted than the average aggregator one-liner and is idiomatic of Alan Cohen's prose, which raises my confidence that it is genuinely his and not a floating anonymous line. I still cannot place it in a specific title — his books on people-pleasing and contentment are the likeliest home but I will not name one as a citation without being able to confirm it.

Attributed to Alan Cohen and consistent with his voice and his frequent play on conventional life-stage language. No primary source identifiable; the only visible provenance is quote-aggregator repetition, which is not evidence.

results.earliest_print_source: Nature, Man and Woman, Alan Watts, 1958
results.notes: Genuine Alan Watts, and unusually well sourced for him: this passage is consistently cited to Nature, Man and Woman (1958), and I recall it appearing in the sourced (not the 'attributed') portion of his Wikiquote entry. The argument — that purposiveness makes the senses miss the world, and that purposelessness is receptive — is a central thesis of that book, and the extended paragraph form is authentic Watts prose rather than a lecture-transcript fragment. Marked attributed rather than verified only because I cannot confirm the page from memory.

Authentically Watts in both idea and image. The self-referential-impossibility metaphor is one he used repeatedly in variant forms — biting your own teeth, seeing your own eyes, lifting yourself by your own bootstraps, the knife that cannot cut itself — deployed against the notion of a self that can stand outside itself and define itself. The attribution to Watts is strong on internal evidence and consistent citation. I cannot pin it to a particular book or lecture, however; many circulating Watts lines come from recorded talks that were later transcribed, so no print source is offered.

results.earliest_print_source: "Retour à Tipasa", in L'Été, Albert Camus, 1954 (essay first published 1952)
results.notes: Genuine Camus, from the essay 'Retour à Tipasa' ('Return to Tipasa'), collected in L'Été (Summer, 1954). Original French: 'Au milieu de l'hiver, j'apprenais enfin qu'il y avait en moi un été invincible.' Note the English here is the loose popular rendering; a closer translation is 'In the midst of winter, I finally learned that there was in me an invincible summer.' The substitution of 'I found' for 'I learned at last' and the stray comma before 'an invincible summer' are artifacts of quote-site transmission, so the attribution is verified but the wording is a paraphrase of the standard translation.

results.earliest_print_source: The Fall (La Chute), Albert Camus, 1956, trans. Justin O'Brien
results.notes: From The Fall (La Chute, 1956), spoken by the narrator Jean-Baptiste Clamence in his monologue about the pleasures of his earlier life. The diction ('to sooth one another mutually', 'condemn such joys as selfishness') is the Justin O'Brien English translation. Important context for corpus use: this is a fictional character's self-justifying confession, not Camus speaking in his own voice — Clamence is an unreliable narrator and the novel is an indictment of exactly this posture. Attribution to Camus as author is sound; presenting it as Camus's personal counsel would misread it.

One of the most-repeated Einstein lines and not found in his writings in this form. What Einstein actually said is documented: in a May 1946 telegram from the Emergency Committee of Atomic Scientists, quoted in the New York Times, 'a new type of thinking is essential if mankind is to survive and move toward higher levels.' The popular 'we cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them' is a much later compression, appearing in management and self-help literature decades afterward, and it is treated as unsourced in the Einstein quotation scholarship (Calaprice's collections place this family of sayings outside the verified material). Kept as attributed_unverified rather than apocryphal because a genuine Einstein statement sits at the root of the paraphrase — but the sentence as written should not be quoted as his words.

No evidence Einstein said or wrote this; it is a standard entry in the misattributed-Einstein lists and does not appear in his published papers, letters, or interviews. The nearest documented ancestor belongs to Ernest Rutherford, reported as saying that a physical theory is no good unless you can explain it to a barmaid — a remark recorded secondhand and itself imperfectly sourced. Similar sentiments are also attributed to Feynman. The Einstein version appears to be a late-twentieth-century construction with no traceable origin, so no true author can be named.

Circulated as Einstein's 'Three Rules of Work.' No primary source exists — it does not appear in his papers or correspondence, and the triad structure is characteristic of twentieth-century motivational compilation rather than of Einstein's prose. The third clause, 'in the middle of difficulty lies opportunity,' is the oldest and most widely repeated of the three and appears in Einstein quotation collections under attributed-but-unsourced headings; even that one has no located primary text. Treat the whole triad as unverified.

A well-documented misattribution, usually circulated in the longer form beginning 'Everybody is a genius. But if you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree...'. It appears nowhere in Einstein's writings and is absent from the scholarly Einstein quotation collections; researchers tracing it have found no instance in his lifetime, with the saying surfacing in this shape only in recent decades. The same pedagogical point is made in George Reavis's fable 'The Animal School' (circulated from around 1940), which is a thematic analogue rather than a demonstrated source. No credible author can be identified.

Attributed to Alan Cohen and compatible with his relationship writing, but this is a generic self-help formulation ('X is not something that happens to you, it is something you choose') that recurs verbatim in many authors' work about love, happiness, and success. The template is too common for the wording alone to establish authorship, and no source can be located.

The recorded author appears to be a confusion of two different Dutch writers. My recollection places this line with J.J. van der Leeuw (Jacobus Johannes van der Leeuw, 1893-1934), the Dutch theosophical writer, in his book The Conquest of Illusion (1928), whose opening pages frame life as a mystery to be lived rather than a problem to be solved. Aart van der Leeuw (1876-1931) was a separate Dutch poet and novelist, and the surname collision is the likely origin of the swap. The quote is also frequently and wrongly attributed to Frank Herbert via Dune, and to various others, which shows how loose its circulation is. I hold the J.J. van der Leeuw reattribution at moderate confidence only — the confidence value given reflects the weak standing of the recorded 'Aart' attribution. Do not promote without checking the 1928 text.
results.suggested_reattribution: J.J. van der Leeuw (Jacobus Johannes van der Leeuw), The Conquest of Illusion (1928) — moderate confidence, needs confirmation against the text

results.notes: The imagery ('dismal dream of limitation', 'the eagle of your sacred visions') is distinctly Alan Cohen's devotional register and closely echoes the A Course in Miracles vocabulary he works within, which supports his authorship. Still no locatable book, chapter, or dated source; his aphorisms of this kind typically originate in daily-inspiration mailings that leave no citable print record.

Sounds authentically like Alan Watts speaking rather than writing — the clipped fragments and the spoken-register repetition are typical of his recorded lectures, and the point (that 'you' and 'I' are shared pronouns naming the same universal subject) is one he made often. But precisely because it reads as transcript, I cannot tie it to a specific talk, recording, or published text, and lecture transcriptions of Watts circulate in many loosely edited versions. Plausibly genuine, wording unverified.

The line reads like a translation of Camus ('j'etais absent au moment ou je prenais le plus de place') and is thematically consistent with the self-accusing narrator of La Chute (The Fall, 1956) or the Carnets. I cannot place it in a specific work or confirm the translation, and I will not name a book I am not sure of. Attribution to Camus is plausible and consistently made, but unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: Farewell Address at Springfield, Illinois, February 11, 1861; Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, Vol. IV
results.notes: Genuine Lincoln, from the Springfield farewell remarks delivered on departing for Washington. The documented wording is 'Without the assistance of that Divine Being, who ever attended him, I cannot succeed. With that assistance I cannot fail.' The corpus text is a lightly trimmed version of that sentence; the substance and the source event are secure.

A very widely repeated Lincoln line, but it rests on later recollection rather than a contemporaneous document. It circulates via post-assassination memoirs and religious biographies of Lincoln, and reference works generally file it under attributed rather than sourced. Lincoln is a known misattribution magnet, so I am holding this below the promotion bar; the sentiment fits his recorded remarks about religion, but no primary source is in my knowledge.

'Adept Godrakpa' is the distinctive rendering used for Gotsangpa Gonpo Dorje (1189-1258), the Tibetan Kagyu yogi, in Cyrus Stearns' translation of his songs of realization published by Wisdom Publications around 2000. The imagery (body like spring mist, mind like empty sky, thoughts like breezes) and the three-point contemplative structure match that body of doggerel-song instruction closely, so the attribution is probably right. I am not certain enough of the exact page or the exact translated wording to record a print citation, so the source field stays null.

Alan Cohen is a prolific inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, Wisdom of the Heart) whose aphorisms circulate through books, newsletters, and daily-quote services with consistent attribution but almost never with a book-and-page citation. Attribution is plausible and uncontested; no primary source in my knowledge.

Same situation as the other Alan Cohen aphorisms in this batch: consistently attributed to him across quote collections, no traceable first appearance in my knowledge. Nothing suggests a different author; the uncertainty is about sourcing, not about who wrote it.

Widely circulated as Alan Cohen, typically without citation. The left-brain/right-brain framing places it in the late-twentieth-century self-help idiom he writes in, which is consistent with the attribution, but I cannot locate a specific book or column.

Attributed to Alan Cohen wherever I have seen it, with no source given. Short enough and aphoristic enough that provenance drift is easy; I have no evidence of an earlier or different author, but no evidence for the attribution beyond repetition either.

Attributed to Alan Cohen without citation. Worth flagging that the idea, and nearly the phrasing, is central to Anthony de Mello's Awareness ('spirituality means waking up... most people are asleep and don't know it'), so this may be a restatement of de Mello that acquired Cohen's name, or a genuine Cohen line in the same lineage. I cannot tell which, so I am not proposing a reattribution.

Consistently attributed to Alan Cohen and one of his more frequently reproduced lines, which slightly strengthens the attribution, but I can point to no book, essay, or dated appearance. Sourcing unverified.
Attributed to Alan Cohen in quote collections with no citation. Voice and vocabulary are consistent with his other work; nothing more than that supports it.

This is a Buddhist scriptural formula, not an Alan Watts original. The line 'Things are not what they seem, nor are they otherwise' is a well-known rendering from the Lankavatara Sutra, and Watts quoted this kind of formulation in his writing on Zen and Mahayana. Attributing it to Watts credits the popularizer rather than the source. My confidence is in the Lankavatara provenance of the formula; I cannot confirm which translation this exact English wording comes from, and it is possible Watts's own paraphrase is what circulates.
results.suggested_reattribution: Lankavatara Sutra (as quoted/paraphrased by Alan Watts)

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Isham Reavis, November 5, 1855; Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, Vol. II
results.notes: Genuine Lincoln, from the letter of advice to Isham Reavis, a young man who had asked about studying law. The documented wording is 'Always bear in mind that your own resolution to succeed, is more important than any other one thing'; the corpus text drops 'other'. I am confident about the letter and the recipient; consider restoring the original wording.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Principles of Research', address at Max Planck's 60th birthday celebration, Physical Society, Berlin, 1918; reprinted in Ideas and Opinions (1954)
results.notes: Authentic Einstein from the 1918 Planck birthday address, one of his best-documented statements about how physical theory is actually arrived at. Original reads 'no logical way to the discovery of these elemental laws'; the corpus text drops 'these'. Source and occasion are secure.

I cannot place this in Alan Watts's books or recorded talks. The idea (a mind in its natural state, unfixed and therefore able to respond in any direction) is standard mushin/wu-hsin material that Watts wrote about in The Way of Zen, and the phrasing also resembles English renderings of Takuan Soho's The Unfettered Mind, which Watts drew on. That makes the attribution plausible but unsupported. Possibly a paraphrase of Watts rather than his words.

No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or interviews that I know of; reference compilations of Einstein quotations treat it as attributed rather than sourced.
