The sentiment closely tracks a documented Niels Bohr remark to Wolfgang Pauli ('we are all agreed that your theory is crazy; the question is whether it is crazy enough to have a chance of being correct'), and this may be a compressed folk version of that exchange re-badged with Einstein's name. I cannot establish the true origin, so no reattribution.

This reads as authentic Einstein prose and I recall it from collections of his writings on the religious feeling of the scientist, associated with his early-1930s credo material ('Mein Glaubensbekenntnis' / The World As I See It). The distinctive cadence and the 'neither evolution nor eternity, only being' close are hard to fake and are consistent with his German essays in translation. I am confident enough in authorship to call it attributed, but I cannot pin the exact essay or year, so I am leaving the citation null and staying under the promotion bar.

I have no record of this in Einstein's writings, and it sits awkwardly against his documented positions, which consistently favour inquiry over belief and reject the 'better to believe' framing as such. It circulates mainly through quotation websites. Einstein is the single largest misattribution magnet in the corpus; absent any source, this should not be promoted.

I believe this is authentic Einstein, from his mid-1930s statements collected in The World As I See It / Mein Weltbild, and it is quoted with consistent wording in serious Einstein compilations rather than only on quote sites. The phrase 'love and devotion towards men and towards objective things' is a characteristic translation of his German. I cannot confirm the specific essay or letter, so the citation stays null and I am holding below 0.80.

Authentic Einstein as far as I know it. The fuller passage continues 'It cannot lead, it can only serve; and it is not fastidious in its choice of a leader', and it appears in the standard English collections of his essays (Ideas and Opinions / Out of My Later Years). The extended, coherent context is good evidence of genuineness. I am not certain enough which original essay or year it comes from to record an earliest print source, so it sits just under the promotion bar pending a human check against Ideas and Opinions.

Almost certainly a paraphrase rather than Einstein's words. What is documented is his 1946 campaign for atomic-age rethinking: 'The unleashed power of the atom has changed everything save our modes of thinking, and thus we drift toward unparalleled catastrophe', and 'a new type of thinking is essential if mankind is to survive'. This line compresses that into modern self-help phrasing. No source for this exact wording. Closely related to q_0243 below, which is the better-known version of the same drift.

One of the most-repeated Einstein misattributions and a documented case of quote drift. It has no source in Einstein's writings; the wording appears in late-twentieth-century management, therapy, and self-help literature and was retro-attributed to him, evolving out of his genuine 1946 remarks about needing a new mode of thinking in the atomic age. Quote-investigation work and the standard Einstein quotation reference both place it in the unsourced/misattributed category. No identifiable individual author, so apocryphal rather than a reattribution.

I am fairly confident this is authentic. The German original is known ('Wer sich als Richter auf dem Gebiete der Wahrheit und Erkenntnis aufzuwerfen unternimmt, wird vom Gelaechter der Goetter zerschmettert'), which is strong evidence against a modern English-language invention, and it is generally dated to an Einstein aphorism of the early 1950s. I cannot confirm the publication it first appeared in, so no citation and no promotion; a human check against the standard Einstein quotation reference should settle it.

Consistently attributed to Einstein and compatible with his documented views on social obligation ('a hundred times every day I remind myself that my inner and outer life are based on the labors of other men'), but I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his writings or interviews. The plain, proverbial phrasing is the kind that attracts famous names. Attribution plausible, sourcing absent.

Correctly pre-flagged. There is no Einstein source for this; it does not appear in his published writings, letters, or interviews, and the standard Einstein quotation reference lists it among sayings attributed to him without support. Attributions to Einstein surface long after his death and appear to be a rebadging of an older inspirational commonplace. No identifiable original author, so apocryphal.

results.earliest_print_source: Relativity: The Special and the General Theory, Albert Einstein, 1916 (German); English translation 1920, Chapter VII
results.notes: This is the opening sentence of Chapter VII ('The Apparent Incompatibility of the Law of Propagation of Light with the Principle of Relativity') of Einstein's own popular exposition Relativity: The Special and the General Theory. Einstein wrote the book himself, so this is a primary source in his own words rather than a reported remark. Wording matches the standard Robert W. Lawson English translation.

Consistently attributed to Einstein and entirely consonant with his documented pacifist writings of the late 1920s and 1930s, where the force-versus-understanding contrast recurs. I cannot place the specific document from memory — candidates I associate with it (a c. 1930 pacifist statement, the material collected in Mein Weltbild / The World As I See It, or the Einstein on Peace compilation) are recollections I am not confident enough to print as a citation, so I have left the source field null rather than guess. Kept below the promotion bar for that reason.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Geometrie und Erfahrung' ('Geometry and Experience'), address to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, Berlin, 27 January 1921
results.notes: One of the best-documented Einstein lines. Delivered in his 1921 Prussian Academy address on geometry and experience and reprinted in Ideas and Opinions (1954). The corpus text drops the semicolon-and joining the two clauses but is otherwise the standard translation.

No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or recorded conversations. This is a stock item in the unsourced/misattributed section of the Einstein Wikiquote page. It surfaces in motivational compilations decades after his death and reads as a modern aphorism rather than a translation from German. It is likely a compressed echo of his genuine 'Imagination is more important than knowledge' (Viereck interview, 1929), but the 'A to B' phrasing is not his. I cannot identify who actually coined it.

Heavily circulated in vegetarian advocacy literature but not found in Einstein's collected writings or correspondence; it appears in the misattributed material on the Einstein Wikiquote page. Einstein's authentic statements on the subject are different and much more qualified — the 1930 letter to Hermann Huth ('Although I have been prevented by outward circumstances from observing a strictly vegetarian diet, I have long been an adherent to the cause in principle') and a 1954 letter to Hans Muehsam written after he adopted the diet on medical advice. The sweeping 'survival of life on Earth' framing is not his idiom. True coiner unknown to me.

Very widely attributed, including in education scholarship, and a German original circulates ('Es ist die wichtigste Kunst des Lehrers, die Freude am Schaffen und Erkennen zu wecken'), which is mild evidence of genuine provenance rather than a back-translated invention. But I cannot place a primary document. It is plausibly connected to his writings and addresses on education (e.g. the 1936 Albany address 'On Education'), yet I do not actually recall it in that text, and some Einstein quote scholarship files lines of this kind as unsourced. Honest verdict: probably his, not demonstrable from what I know.

The joke is authentically Einstein's — it was his stock popular gloss on relativity, given to reporters (his secretary Helen Dukas handed out a version of it) and recorded in multiple accounts from the late 1920s onward. Two cautions. First, this specific wording ('courting a nice girl', 'red-hot cinder') is one of several circulating variants; the more commonly documented form is 'When you sit with a nice girl for two hours it seems like a minute; when you sit on a hot stove for a minute it seems like two hours.' Second, the citation often attached to it online — 'Journal of Exothermic Science and Technology (JEST), Vol. 1, No. 9, 1938' — is a spoof, not a real journal, so I have deliberately not printed it. Substance solid, exact wording and source not verifiable.

results.earliest_print_source: 'The Common Language of Science', radio address recorded for the British Association for the Advancement of Science, 28 September 1941; reprinted in Out of My Later Years (1950) and Ideas and Opinions (1954)
results.notes: This is the closing sentence of Einstein's short 1941 broadcast on the common language of science. Written by Einstein for delivery, so a primary source. Corpus text matches the standard printed version including the parenthetical dashes.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Morris Raphael Cohen, 19 March 1940, written in support of Bertrand Russell's appointment at the College of the City of New York
results.notes: Genuine and well documented. Einstein wrote it to philosopher Morris Raphael Cohen during the public campaign against Russell's teaching appointment. Despite being a heavily meme-ified line, this one survives scrutiny — the letter is real and the context is specific.

results.earliest_print_source: Small Is Beautiful: A Study of Economics as if People Mattered, E. F. Schumacher, 1973
results.notes: I do not believe this is Einstein's. I recall it from E. F. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful (1973), where the wording runs 'Any intelligent fool can make things bigger, more complex, and more violent. It takes a touch of genius — and a lot of courage — to move in the opposite direction.' Note that the corpus version has dropped 'intelligent', which is the tell of a quote that has passed through attribution drift. Caveat on my own certainty: I am confident the line is Schumacher's in print and not Einstein's, but less certain whether Schumacher coined it or was himself echoing an earlier source, so treat the reattribution as probable rather than settled.

results.earliest_print_source: Esther Salaman, 'A Talk With Einstein', The Listener, vol. 54 (1955)
results.notes: This is a compression of a longer remark Einstein made to the physicist Esther Salaman around 1925, which she published from memory in 1955: 'I want to know how God created this world. I am not interested in this or that phenomenon, in the spectrum of this or that element. I want to know His thoughts; the rest are details.' So the source is a recollection recorded roughly thirty years after the conversation, and the popular one-sentence form here is an editor's condensation rather than Einstein's own sentence. Genuine in substance; the exact wording is not.

results.earliest_print_source: George Sylvester Viereck, 'What Life Means to Einstein', The Saturday Evening Post, 26 October 1929 (republished in Glimpses of the Great, 1930)
results.notes: I recall this from the 1929 Viereck interview, the same conversation that produced 'Imagination is more important than knowledge.' The 'gift of fantasy' phrasing is characteristic of that interview's translation. Hedge: I am confident about the interview but not about the exact page, and I cannot rule out that the line comes from a neighbouring Viereck piece rather than the Saturday Evening Post printing itself — hence attributed rather than verified, and held below the promotion bar pending a human check against the printed interview.

Widely quoted and thoroughly consistent with Einstein's documented statements about intuition preceding reasoning (the Viereck interview, the Wertheimer conversations, the Hadamard survey on mathematical invention). But I cannot place a primary source for this exact sentence, and lines of this shape are exactly the kind that get retrofitted onto Einstein by inspirational compilers. I have a faint association with a mid-century popular biography, but it is too faint to print as a citation. Plausible but unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Robert S. Marcus, 12 February 1950 (Albert Einstein Archives 60-424); widely reprinted, including in the New York Post, 28 November 1972
results.notes: The genuine article. Einstein wrote this in a condolence letter to Robert S. Marcus, political director of the World Jewish Congress, after the death of Marcus's son. The archival letter exists, which is why this passage survives scrutiny where its New Age paraphrases do not. Two small textual notes: the original reads 'a part of the whole' rather than 'a part of a whole' and 'widening our circles of compassion'; the ellipsis in the corpus text elides 'as something separated from the rest' into the following clause. Worth normalising against the archive text.

I am fairly confident this is genuine Einstein on death and the individual life. I associate it with his spoken credo of autumn 1932 ('Mein Glaubensbekenntnis', recorded for the German League of Human Rights) and with the material collected in Dukas and Hoffmann's Albert Einstein: The Human Side. The variant wording I recall is closer to 'so much a part of everything living ... the concrete existence of any one person in this eternal flow', which suggests the corpus text is a different translation of the same German. Because I cannot settle which of those two sources carries it, I have left the print source null rather than guess between them.

This is a degraded paraphrase of the authentic 1950 letter to Robert S. Marcus, which the corpus already holds correctly as q_0260. The giveaways are 'self-imposed prison' and 'to find the reality of oneness' — neither phrase is in Einstein's letter; the original says the delusion 'is a kind of prison for us' and that our task is 'widening our circles of compassion to embrace all living creatures and the whole of nature in its beauty.' The oneness formulation entered circulation through later spiritual literature. Recommendation for the human reviewer: this is a duplicate of q_0260 in corrupted form and should be dropped in favour of the archival wording, not promoted alongside it.

A loose popular restatement of the same Salaman-reported remark behind q_0257 ('I want to know how God created this world ... I want to know His thoughts; the rest are details', The Listener, 1955). The 'All I want to do is learn to think like God thinks' wording is not attested in Einstein's own words or in Salaman's account; it reads as a paraphrase of a paraphrase. Duplicative of q_0257, which is the better-supported form of the same line.

Long-standing and consistent attribution, and the vocabulary ('illimitable superior spirit', 'frail and feeble mind') matches Einstein's cosmic-religion register closely enough that I think it is genuine — compare the verified 1936 Phyllis Wright letter at q_0265, which says something very similar. I cannot place the primary document, however. It circulates in the standard Einstein compilations with varying and sometimes absent citations, and I do not want to pick one from memory. Probably genuine, source unplaced.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Phyllis Wright, 24 January 1936 (Albert Einstein Archives 42-601); reprinted in Albert Einstein: The Human Side, ed. Helen Dukas and Banesh Hoffmann
results.notes: Written to Phyllis Wright, a sixth-grade student at the Riverside Church in New York who had asked Einstein whether scientists pray. The archival letter is well documented and this passage is quoted from it accurately. Corpus text splits 'Every one' where the letter reads 'everyone', a trivial variant.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Religion and Science', The New York Times Magazine, 9 November 1930; reprinted in Ideas and Opinions (1954)
results.notes: From Einstein's own signed essay 'Religion and Science', where he sets out the third stage of religious feeling — the cosmic religious sense of the scientist. A primary source in his own words. The corpus text matches the standard English printing.

results.earliest_print_source: The Metaphoric Mind: A Celebration of Creative Consciousness, Bob Samples, 1976
results.notes: A well-known misattribution and one I am confident about. Bob Samples wrote a loose gloss on Einstein — approximately 'Albert Einstein called the intuitive or metaphoric mind a sacred gift. He added that the rational mind was a faithful servant. It is paradoxical that in the context of modern life we have begun to worship the servant and defile the divine' — and that commentary was subsequently quoted back as if it were Einstein's own sentence. The 'sacred gift / faithful servant / honors the servant and has forgotten the gift' formulation is Samples' prose, not Einstein's, and no such passage exists in Einstein's writings. Recommend reattribution or removal.

No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or reported conversations that I know of. It appears in late-twentieth-century quotation compilations attached to his name, which is the standard signature of an Einstein-magnet aphorism. I cannot identify a true origin either, so I am not offering a reattribution. Honest answer: unknown, and almost certainly not his.

results.earliest_print_source: George Sylvester Viereck interview with Einstein, 1929–1930 (published as 'What Life Means to Einstein', The Saturday Evening Post, 26 October 1929, and in Glimpses of the Great, 1930)
results.notes: The child-in-the-library metaphor is genuinely Einstein's and is documented from his conversations with Viereck; the version I recall runs 'We are in the position of a little child entering a huge library whose walls are covered to the ceiling with books in many different tongues ... The child notes a definite plan in the arrangement of the books, a mysterious order which it does not comprehend, but only dimly suspects. That, it seems to me, is the attitude of the human mind, even the greatest and most cultured, toward God.' Caveats: the corpus text is a reported conversation, not something Einstein wrote, and its opening sentence ('The human mind is not capable of grasping the Universe') plus the truncated ending differ from the rendering I know. Attributed rather than verified because I cannot confirm which printing carries this exact wording.

results.earliest_print_source: Albert Einstein: The Human Side, ed. Helen Dukas and Banesh Hoffmann (1979)
results.notes: I recall this from the Dukas and Hoffmann collection of Einstein's personal correspondence, drawn from a letter or reply written in his last years (mid-1950s), and continuing past the ellipsis to say that this feeling has nothing to do with mysticism. Dukas was his secretary and the collection works from the archive, so the chain is good. Hedge: I am confident about the collection but not about the exact letter, recipient, or date, so I have named only the book and left the specifics out rather than invent them. Held below the promotion bar pending a page-level check.

Widely attributed to Einstein in quotation collections and compatible with his 'true religiosity' language, but I cannot place a primary source. The phrasing is noticeably plainer than his usual translated register, which makes me slightly wary that it is a paraphrase of a longer passage rather than a sentence he wrote. Not enough for me to call it misattributed, not nearly enough to promote. Uncertain.

results.earliest_print_source: "What I Believe", Albert Einstein, Forum and Century vol. 84 (1930); reprinted in The World As I See It / Mein Weltbild (1934-35)
results.notes: Genuine Einstein passage from his 1930 credo essay 'What I Believe'. The canonical translation reads 'The most beautiful experience we can have is the mysterious. It is the fundamental emotion which stands at the cradle of true art and true science...' The wording here ('the finest emotion of which we are capable is the mystic emotion... the germ of all art and all true science') is a different, older English rendering that circulates widely, notably via Lincoln Barnett's The Universe and Dr. Einstein (1948). Content, structure, and closing sentence ('in this sense, and in this sense alone, I rank myself among profoundly religious men') all match the authentic essay. Verified as Einstein; the exact English wording is translation-dependent.

Consistent with Einstein's 1930s social essays and commonly cited to him; I recall the line in the orbit of The World As I See It (1934) but cannot place the specific essay or page from memory, so I am not supplying a citation. Not one of the classic Einstein fakes (no self-help cadence, no science-vs-religion punchline), and the sentiment matches his repeated writing on the individual's obligation to community. Plausible but unconfirmed at the primary-source level.

results.earliest_print_source: LSD: My Problem Child (LSD - Mein Sorgenkind), Albert Hofmann, 1979 (English translation 1980)
results.notes: Authentic Hofmann, from LSD: My Problem Child - it appears in the framing material where he sets out why he wrote the book. The 'materialistic, dualistic belief that people and their environment are separate' / 'oneness with animate nature and all of creation' language is verbatim Hofmann and is one of the most-quoted passages in the book. NOTE: the author's name is misspelled in the corpus - it is Albert Hofmann (one 'f' at the end, two total), the Sandoz chemist who first synthesized LSD, not 'Albert Hoffman'.

This is a floating self-help aphorism with two competing attributions and no primary source under either. It is far more commonly attributed to William James ('The greatest discovery of my generation is that a human being can alter his life by altering his attitudes of mind'), and that James version is a known unverified attribution - it does not appear in James's published works and surfaces in mid-20th-century inspirational literature. The Schweitzer variant ('of any generation') looks like downstream drift from the James version. Neither attribution is supportable; I cannot identify the true originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: Civilization and Ethics (Kultur und Ethik), Albert Schweitzer, 1923 - The Philosophy of Civilization, Part II
results.notes: This is Schweitzer's core statement of Ehrfurcht vor dem Leben (reverence for life) and is a genuine passage from his ethics volume, where he defines the ethical man as one for whom all life is sacred and who helps all life in need. Schweitzer restates it in Out of My Life and Thought (1931). Confident in the author and the work; slight residual uncertainty only on chapter/page and translation wording.

This is a loose paraphrase of a line widely attributed to Schweitzer in the form 'I don't know what your destiny will be, but one thing I know: the only ones among you who will be really happy are those who will have sought and found how to serve.' Even that canonical form has no confirmed primary source - it is usually reported secondhand as advice to students, without a traceable speech or text. The wording given here ('what path in life you will take... you will never be happy') is a further-degraded retelling. The sentiment is authentically Schweitzerian, but neither the wording nor the source can be verified.

Genuinely Schweitzer's, to the best of my knowledge; the standard translation runs 'Sometimes our light goes out but is blown into flame again by an encounter with another human being. Each of us owes deepest thanks to those who have rekindled this inner light.' I recall it being sourced to Memoirs of Childhood and Youth (1924), but I am not confident enough in that placement to record it as a citation. The version in the corpus is a rephrasing ('our inner fire goes out', 'burst into flame'). Attribution good, exact source and wording unconfirmed.

A signature Szent-Gyorgyi line, consistently attributed to him across scientific and popular literature and entirely in his idiom. It is usually sourced to his contribution to I. J. Good's anthology The Scientist Speculates (1962), but I cannot confirm that placement precisely enough to record it as a citation. NOTE: the author's name is garbled in the corpus - the correct form is Albert Szent-Gyorgyi (Hungarian Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine, 1937; full name Albert von Szent-Gyorgyi Nagyrapolt), not 'Albert von Szent-Gyorgy'.

I cannot place this in Huxley's work, and the aphoristic snap of it is unlike his prose, which is discursive even when epigrammatic. It sits in a family of interchangeable aging aphorisms whose attributions rotate freely - compare 'Nobody grows old merely by living a number of years; we grow old by deserting our ideals' (Samuel Ullman) and 'We do not stop playing because we grow old; we grow old because we stop playing' (attributed variously to Oliver Wendell Holmes and George Bernard Shaw, unverified in both). No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know who said it.

Authentic Huxley, from the last years of his life (c. 1961-62) - the self-deprecating cadence and the phrase 'the human problem' are characteristic, and the remark is well documented in the Huxley literature as a summing-up he offered near the end. It is usually reported from a late lecture or interview rather than from something he wrote, and I cannot fix the specific occasion or the secondary source that first printed it, so I am leaving the citation null. Attribution strong, provenance of the report unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: Texts and Pretexts: An Anthology with Commentaries, Aldous Huxley, 1932
results.notes: Genuine Huxley, from the opening pages of Texts and Pretexts. Original wording: 'Experience is not what happens to a man; it is what a man does with what happens to him.' The corpus version is a modernized second-person rendering of the same sentence. Frequently misattributed elsewhere to Carl Jung and to Anthony Robbins-style paraphrasers, but Huxley is the source.

results.earliest_print_source: "A Case of Voluntary Ignorance", Aldous Huxley, in Collected Essays (1959); essay first published 1956
results.notes: Authentic Huxley, from the essay 'A Case of Voluntary Ignorance', collected in Collected Essays (1959) after appearing in his mid-1950s essay work. The self-swallowing structure of the sentence is quoted accurately in the corpus. Confident in author and essay; mild uncertainty on first-publication venue and date.

This is Huxley's central thesis about means and ends and reads as authentically his - the argument that means determine ends is the spine of his 1937 book Ends and Means, written under Gerald Heard's and the pacifist movement's influence. The standard attribution points to Ends and Means (1937), but I cannot confirm this exact sentence pair appears there rather than in a related essay or in his Gandhi commentary, so I am not recording a citation. Attribution to Huxley is sound; the specific work is unconfirmed.

Alex Grey is a living visionary artist and the passage is squarely in his register - the cosmic-evolutionary framing of creativity and the phrase 'the redemptive mission of art' echo his book The Mission of Art (1998) and his lecture material. But I cannot place this specific wording in a published text or talk, and contemporary artist statements circulate heavily paraphrased on social media. Plausibly authentic, unconfirmed.

Standardly attributed to Alexandre Dumas fils in 20th-century quotation dictionaries ('Toutes les generalisations sont dangereuses, y compris celle-ci'), but I know of no primary source in his plays or novels, and quotation dictionaries of that era propagated attributions without sourcing. A close cousin, 'No generalization is wholly true, not even this one', is attributed to Oliver Wendell Holmes - the two may share an origin or may be independent formulations of an old joke. NOTE: if this attribution is kept, the corpus name should be 'Alexandre Dumas' (fils), not the anglicized 'Alexander Dumas'.

I cannot place this in either Dumas pere or Dumas fils. It circulates on aggregator sites credited to a bare 'Alexandre Dumas', which is a common pattern for orphaned motivational lines - the enlist-against-yourself conceit reads more like 19th-century moralist or later self-help prose than like Dumas's narrative voice, though I would not call it a misattribution without evidence of a different author. No traceable source. NOTE: the corpus name is anglicized ('Alexander'); the French author is Alexandre Dumas, and which Dumas is intended is itself unclear.

This reaches modern readers through Napoleon Hill, who quotes it as Alexander Graham Bell in Think and Grow Rich (1937) - I am fairly but not fully confident of that placement, so I have not recorded it as a citation. The material point is that Hill is an unreliable transmitter: his claimed interviews with and quotations from Carnegie, Edison, Bell and others have been repeatedly challenged, and several are undocumented outside his own books. I know of no Bell letter, lecture, or notebook containing this sentence. Treat the attribution as weak pending a primary source.

Alexander Isley is a real and identifiable graphic designer (founding art director of Spy magazine, later Alexander Isley Inc.), and the line has the flavor of design-school advice given in an AIGA talk or a published list of maxims for young designers - the kind of source that rarely makes it into quotation records. I cannot confirm the wording or the occasion. Attribution plausible and specific enough not to look invented, but unverified.

Very likely genuine Pope, from the aphorism collection Thoughts on Various Subjects (first published 1727 in the Pope-Swift Miscellanies), where the sentence runs closer to 'Some people will never learn anything, for this reason, because they understand everything too soon.' Two caveats keep this below verified: the Miscellanies were a joint Pope-Swift production and individual maxims are sometimes disputed between them, and the corpus text is a compressed modernization with an ellipsis rather than the original wording.

results.earliest_print_source: An Essay on Criticism, Alexander Pope, 1711 (Part II, line 525)
results.notes: One of the best-documented lines in English poetry. Pope's couplet reads 'Good-nature and good-sense must ever join; / To err is human, to forgive, divine.' Primary source is unambiguous.

results.earliest_print_source: The Gulag Archipelago 1918-1956, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, 1973 (Volume 1, Part I, Chapter 4, "The Bluecaps")
results.notes: Authentic and correctly quoted, from the celebrated passage in 'The Bluecaps'. The full passage continues past what is quoted here ('During the life of any heart this line keeps changing place...'). Text matches the Whitney/Willetts English translation closely. NOTE: the corpus uses the anglicized 'Alexander'; the standard transliteration is Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn.

results.earliest_print_source: Dialogues of Alfred North Whitehead, as recorded by Lucien Price, 1954
results.notes: Genuine Whitehead, recorded by Lucien Price. The full remark is 'There are no whole truths; all truths are half-truths. It is trying to treat them as whole truths that plays the devil.' The corpus quotes only the middle clause, which is the form that circulates. Source is a recorded conversation rather than Whitehead's own pen, but Price's Dialogues is an accepted and dated primary record.

results.earliest_print_source: Adventures of Ideas, Alfred North Whitehead, 1933
results.notes: Consistent with Whitehead's treatment of Adventure as a civilizing force in the final part of Adventures of Ideas, where he argues that art and civilization decay without the sense of adventure. I am confident in the author and reasonably confident in the book; the exact wording circulates in two forms ('when there is' / 'where there is'), which suggests some paraphrase drift, so I am holding this just under the verified bar rather than claiming chapter and page.

Almost certainly not Whitehead. The flippant one-liner register is entirely foreign to his prose, and the theological claim contradicts his actual position: Whitehead's process theology in Process and Reality (1929) and Religion in the Making (1926) develops a dipolar God distinct from, though internally related to, the world - he had no interest in the human-as-deity conceit, and he was not an atheist earlier in life in the sense the joke requires. This reads as a modern quip or bumper-sticker line that acquired a philosopher's name for weight. I cannot identify the actual originator, so no reattribution is offered. Recommend removal rather than reassignment.

results.earliest_print_source: Preface to The Dreaded Comparison: Human and Animal Slavery by Marjorie Spiegel, Alice Walker, 1988
results.notes: Authentic Alice Walker, from the preface she wrote for Marjorie Spiegel's The Dreaded Comparison. The parallel she draws between animal exploitation and the ideologies of racial slavery and patriarchy is the explicit argument of that preface, and this is its most-quoted sentence. Correctly attributed and accurately quoted.

Consistently attributed to Alice Walker in quote collections and I have a weak recollection of it appearing in her fiction (possibly The Temple of My Familiar, 1989), but I cannot place the sentence in a specific work with confidence. No competing claimant, so the attribution is plausible; the sourcing is not established.

Widely and consistently attributed to Alice Walker, and the aphoristic-theological turn is characteristic of her essays. I cannot identify the book, essay, or interview it comes from, so I will not name one. Plausible but unsourced.

One of the most-circulated Alice Walker lines, attributed to her with unusual consistency and no rival claimant, which is mild evidence in its favor. But it circulates without a source citation everywhere I have seen it; I cannot place it in a specific book, essay, or speech. Attribution likely correct, provenance unestablished.

Attributed to Alina Wheeler (author of Designing Brand Identity) in most design-quote contexts, but the same line is also circulated as Le Corbusier's, and I cannot confirm either. If it is Wheeler's it would most plausibly come from Designing Brand Identity, but I cannot confirm that it originates with her rather than being quoted by her. Competing attribution keeps confidence low.

I have no knowledge of an author named Allyson Jones associated with this or any quotation, and no recollection of the line itself. No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know where this came from or whether the attributed person exists as a public author.

results.earliest_print_source: Future Shock, Alvin Toffler, 1970 (quoting psychologist Herbert Gerjuoy)
results.notes: Toffler did not originate this. In Future Shock (1970) he quotes psychologist Herbert Gerjuoy: 'The illiterate of the future will not be the person who cannot read. It will be the person who does not know how to learn.' The widely circulated '21st century / learn, unlearn, and relearn' wording is a later popular reshaping of that sentence, not a verbatim Toffler line. Toffler is the transmitter, Gerjuoy the source of the thought; the exact modern wording is of uncertain authorship.
results.suggested_reattribution: Herbert Gerjuoy, as quoted by Alvin Toffler in Future Shock (1970)

results.notes: Very widely attributed to Earhart and consistent with her documented voice on risk and resolve; I believe it derives from her own writing or correspondence, but I cannot place it in a specific book (The Fun of It, Last Flight) or letter, so I will not cite one. Plausible and uncontested, but unsourced in what I know.

Attributed to Earhart in quote collections, but the diction ('Good example is followed', 'throws out roots in all directions, and the roots spring up and make new trees') reads as nineteenth-century moral-essay prose rather than Earhart's plain twentieth-century style, and I cannot place it in any of her writings. I suspect an older, uncredited source that has been re-labelled with a famous name, but I cannot identify that source, so I am not proposing a reattribution. Treat the Earhart attribution as doubtful.

Consistently attributed to Earhart and strongly consistent with her documented statements about accepting the hazards of her flights (compare the pre-1937 'popping-off' letter to G.P. Putnam). I believe it is genuine and comes from her own writing or an interview, most likely around the 1932 Atlantic solo or the 1937 world flight, but I cannot pin the specific text, so no print source is named.

This is a modern internet aphorism with a snappy cadence unlike Earhart's prose, and I know of no source for it in her writings, letters, or contemporary press. Earhart is a magnet for aspirational lines of this kind. Related but distinct older sayings exist (e.g. John Andrew Holmes on never telling a young person a thing cannot be done). Attribution should be treated as very likely apocryphal; I stop short of the 'apocryphal' label only because I cannot demonstrate invention.

results.earliest_print_source: Seduction of the Minotaur, Anaïs Nin, 1961
results.notes: Nin did write a version of this in Seduction of the Minotaur (1961), but she presented it as a saying she was recalling, framed as Talmudic ('we do not see things as they are, we see them as we are'). The maxim is older than Nin and is not actually in the Talmud; variants circulated in English well before 1961. So Nin is a real conduit but not the originator, and the corpus should not present her as the author without that caveat. I cannot name the earliest English printing with confidence.

Consistently cited as Nin's and stylistically hers; standard citations place it in The Diary of Anaïs Nin, though I cannot confirm which volume, so I have not named one. No competing attribution known.

Universally attributed to Nin and usually circulated as part of a short piece titled 'Risk', but its location in her published corpus is contested — I recall ongoing disagreement about whether it appears in the diaries as printed. Note also that the wording here ('There came a time when...') differs from the standard circulating form ('And the day came when the risk to remain tight in a bud...'), which is a marker of a quote that has drifted. Attribution plausible, source not established.

results.earliest_print_source: The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 3 (1939–1944), Anaïs Nin
results.notes: The best-sourced of the Nin lines in this batch: standard references place it in the third volume of the published Diary, in an early-1940s entry, and the attribution is stable across sources. I am citing the volume from recollection of consistent standard citations rather than a checked page, so I hold it just under the primary-source band.

Consistently attributed to Nin and consistent with her recurring reflections on why she kept the diary. Commonly cited to the published Diary (a later volume), but I cannot confirm the volume or the exact wording of the original sentence, and the popular form may be a tightening of a longer passage. No competing claimant.

results.earliest_print_source: Nadja, André Breton, 1928
results.notes: The closing line of Nadja (1928): 'La beauté sera CONVULSIVE ou ne sera pas.' Primary source is secure. The English here is a compressed rendering — the literal sense is 'Beauty will be CONVULSIVE or it will not be [at all]'; the corpus may want the standard translation wording.

results.earliest_print_source: Les Faux-Monnayeurs (The Counterfeiters), André Gide, 1925
results.notes: Genuine Gide, from The Counterfeiters (1925): 'On ne découvre pas de terre nouvelle sans consentir à perdre de vue, d'abord et pour longtemps, tout rivage.' The English here is a faithful translation. This is the authentic original of which q_0314 is the popular corruption.

This popular English wording does not correspond to any sentence Gide wrote. It is a loose, anonymous paraphrase of the Counterfeiters line captured verbatim in q_0313 ('new lands' / 'lose sight of the shore' becoming 'new oceans' / 'courage'). Gide is the source of the thought, not of these words, and the paraphraser is unknown. The corpus already holds the authentic version at q_0313 and should prefer it; this entry is a duplicate in corrupted form.
results.suggested_reattribution: Paraphrase of André Gide, Les Faux-Monnayeurs (1925); paraphraser unknown

results.earliest_print_source: Les Nourritures terrestres (The Fruits of the Earth), André Gide, 1897
results.notes: From the closing envoi of The Fruits of the Earth, addressed to Nathanaël. Standard translations end 'the most irreplaceable of beings' rather than 'of things', and the passage as given has been trimmed of its direct address to Nathanaël — worth normalizing against a published translation. The attribution itself is secure.

Consistently attributed to Andy Grove of Intel in management and communication literature, and the sentiment matches his writing on managerial output. I cannot place it in High Output Management, Only the Paranoid Survive, or a specific talk, so I will not cite one. Plausible, unsourced.

Reads authentically as Andrew Harvey — the vocabulary (journey of return to Origin, the Direct Path, rungs of a ladder made of awareness, Divine Consciousness in self-disguise) is his, and the passage is long and specific enough that it is unlikely to be an invented aphorism. My best guess is one of his comparative-mysticism books, plausibly The Direct Path (2000), but I cannot confirm the title or page, so the source field stays null. Attribution likely correct; citation unestablished.

A classic presidential magnet quote. I know of no primary source in Jackson's speeches, letters, or messages; the attribution appears to be a twentieth-century development, amplified when Robert F. Kennedy quoted it as Jackson's. Older cognate sayings exist in the same family ('One on God's side is a majority'; Thoreau's 'any man more right than his neighbours constitutes a majority of one'), which is how such lines usually accrete. I cannot identify the actual originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution — but the Jackson attribution should be treated as unsupported.

I cannot verify this. The 'Screenwriter' context tag suggests Andrew Schneider of Northern Exposure, but the content is New Age / nondual self-realization writing that fits a different Andrew Schneider (a spiritual teacher and author on cosmic nature) — a likely conflation of two people with the same name. No traceable source for the sentence itself.

Same problem as q_0319: attributed to 'Andrew Schneider' with a 'Screenwriter' context that does not match the content, which reads as contemporary spiritual writing. I cannot place the sentence in any published work and cannot establish which Andrew Schneider is meant. No traceable source.

'Angela Monet' is not an identifiable writer — no book, poem, or biographical record I know of corresponds to the name, and the attribution appears only in late-twentieth-century quote circulation. The same line is very widely misattributed to Nietzsche, where it does not appear in any of his works; that misattribution is well known and unsupported. Both the phantom-author and Nietzsche attributions fail, and I cannot identify a real origin, so this is best treated as of unknown/invented provenance.

Angeles Arrien (1940-2014) was a cultural anthropologist and author of The Four-Fold Way (1993) and The Second Half of Life (2005). The language here — 'the deep wisdom way', silence as territory — is consistent with her idiom, and I have not seen this line attributed to anyone else. But I cannot place it in a specific book, lecture, or interview, and it may be a transcription of spoken teaching rather than a published sentence. No print source located; attribution plausible but unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: Der Cherubinische Wandersmann, Angelus Silesius, 1657
results.notes: This is a rhymed English rendering of a couplet from Angelus Silesius's Cherubinischer Wandersmann (1657), the source of essentially all epigrams circulating under his name. The underlying German couplet is genuine Silesius in theme and form (the paradox of self-emptying making room for God recurs throughout Book I). The specific English wording — with the 'everywhere / aren't there' rhyme — is a translator's construction, and I believe it comes from Stephen Mitchell's anthology The Enlightened Heart (1989), though I am not certain enough of that to record it as the print source. Attribution to Silesius is sound; the exact couplet number and translator are unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: Het Achterhuis (The Diary of a Young Girl), Anne Frank, 1947
results.notes: This line is genuinely from Anne Frank's diary and is listed among her sourced quotations. It is commonly cited to the entry of 26 March 1944, though I cannot confirm that date with confidence, and English wording varies slightly between the Barbara Mooyaart-Doubleday and Susan Massotty translations. Attribution to Anne Frank is well founded; the precise entry and translation are the open questions.

I cannot place this in Anne Lamott's work. Bird by Bird (1994) argues at length for daily writing discipline, so the sentiment is compatible with her, but I have no recollection of this sentence in her books or essays. Variants of 'discipline is the path to freedom' circulate widely without stable attribution (Jocko Willink's 'discipline equals freedom' is the best-known modern form). Possible that a paraphrase of Lamott's ideas has hardened into a quotation. Low confidence.

Consistently attributed to Madame Anne-Sophie Swetchine (1782-1857), the Russian-French salon writer whose maxims were collected posthumously by the Comte de Falloux and translated into English in the 1860s. Lines of hers were heavily mined by late-19th-century American quotation compendia, which is almost certainly how this one entered circulation, and the aphoristic form fits her. I cannot confirm the passage in a specific edition of her writings, so I am not recording a print source. Attribution is old and stable but unverified against a primary text.

A modern mashup, correctly left anonymous. The underlying adage — success is where preparation meets opportunity — is much older and has been attributed to Seneca, Oprah Winfrey, and racing driver Bobby Unser, among others, with no settled origin. The '10,000 hours' framing cannot predate the popularization of Ericsson's deliberate-practice research through Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers (2008), so this specific sentence is a post-2008 recombination. No identifiable author.

This is the widely forwarded 'Hopi Elders' Prophecy' / 'We Are the Ones We've Been Waiting For' text, usually credited to 'the Hopi Nation, Oraibi, Arizona' and dated around 2000-2001, when it spread by email and appeared in New Age and activist anthologies. Its authenticity as a Hopi statement is contested: no named speaker, no recording, no Hopi-published source that I know of, and the diction reads as English-language spiritual-activist prose rather than translated oral teaching. Sometimes loosely associated with Thomas Banyacya, who died in 1999. Treat the tribal attribution as unproven.

An old joke of the bumper-sticker and office-poster variety, circulating for decades in variants ('I thought I was wrong once, but I was mistaken'). The 'anonymous six year old' framing is a storytelling device, not a provenance. No traceable author or first appearance.

Very widely and consistently attributed to Ansel Adams, and squarely consistent with his zone-system philosophy of the photograph as a made object (his 'negative is the score, print is the performance' analogy makes the same point). I cannot place it in a specific book, letter, or interview, and it may be a condensation of a longer passage. Attribution likely correct; primary source not located.

Long and stably attributed to Ansel Adams, and among the more credible Adams sayings — it reflects his documented output standards. Circulates with slight variants ('Twelve significant photographs in any one year is a good crop'). I cannot identify the original interview or publication, so no print source is recorded.

Consistently attributed to Ansel Adams across photography literature and quotation collections; no competing attribution that I know of. The sentiment matches his teaching writings, where he repeatedly resisted formula. No specific book, essay, or interview located, so this stays below the verified bar.

Widely attributed to Ansel Adams and frequently quoted in design and photography contexts. I know of no rival attribution, and the epigram fits his insistence on previsualization. However, I cannot locate it in his published writings (the Basic Photo series, Examples, or the Autobiography), and pithy lines like this are exactly the kind that attach to famous names. Plausible but unsourced.

Attributed to Antony Jay (1930-2016), British writer, co-author of Yes Minister and author of Management and Machiavelli (1967). Note the surname is nearly always given with the spelling 'Antony', not 'Anthony' as in this record. The line appears in management and creativity anthologies with consistent credit to him, but I cannot place it in a specific book or article, and the possibility that it originated in a magazine piece or was condensed from a longer passage is real. Correcting the forename spelling is the main actionable finding.

Consistent with Anthony (Tony) Robbins's core material and widely circulated under his name; the ellipsis and clipped syntax suggest it was transcribed from a seminar or audio program rather than written. Plausibly drawn from Awaken the Giant Within (1991) or the Personal Power tapes, but I cannot confirm either, so no print source is recorded. Attribution likely correct, source unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: Terre des Hommes (Wind, Sand and Stars), Antoine de Saint-Exupery, 1939
results.notes: Genuine and primary-sourced. Original French, from the chapter on the airplane: 'Il semble que la perfection soit atteinte non quand il n'y a plus rien a ajouter, mais quand il n'y a plus rien a retrancher.' The English here is a standard faithful rendering. Note the author name should carry the accent: Antoine de Saint-Exupery -> Saint-Exupery (Saint-Exupéry).

results.earliest_print_source: Citadelle (The Wisdom of the Sands), Antoine de Saint-Exupery, 1948 (posthumous)
results.notes: This popular English sentence is a paraphrase, not a translation. Saint-Exupery wrote a related passage in Citadelle about not assigning men to gather wood but teaching them longing for the vast and endless sea; the crisp leadership-poster version was assembled later and is not a literal rendering of any single line he wrote. Quote Investigator has examined this saying and reached the same conclusion. Keep the attribution but flag it as a paraphrase of Citadelle rather than a quotation.

results.earliest_print_source: Le Petit Prince (The Little Prince), Antoine de Saint-Exupery, 1943, ch. XXI
results.notes: Primary source confirmed: the fox's secret in chapter XXI of Le Petit Prince. Original French: 'On ne voit bien qu'avec le coeur. L'essentiel est invisible pour les yeux.' The English wording here matches the common Katherine Woods-lineage rendering. Author name should carry the accent (Saint-Exupéry).

The motto 'pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will' is genuinely Gramsci's watchword — he used it in L'Ordine Nuovo, in the Prison Notebooks, and in prison letters (notably to his brother Carlo, December 1929, in the form 'I am a pessimist because of intelligence, but an optimist because of will'). Two caveats: Gramsci took the formula from Romain Rolland rather than coining it, and the sentence as given here ('We must fight the pessimism of the intellect with the optimism of the will') is a loose English recasting that inverts his sense — for Gramsci the two are held together, not set against each other. Attribution to Gramsci is sound; the wording is not his.

results.earliest_print_source: Pappus of Alexandria, Synagoge (Mathematical Collection), Book VIII, c. 340 CE
results.notes: The saying does not survive in Archimedes' own writings. It is reported centuries later by Pappus of Alexandria, with the Doric form 'Give me a place to stand and I will move the earth' also cited by Simplicius and echoed by Plutarch's account of Archimedes' demonstrations for Hieron. So: ancient secondary attestation, not a primary source. The phrase 'and a long enough lever' is a modern embellishment — the classical versions ask only for a place to stand (the lever being implied by the surrounding argument). Genuine tradition, embellished wording.

The author name is misspelled: this is almost certainly Arjuna Ardagh, author of The Translucent Revolution (2005) and Awakening Into Oneness, not 'Arduna Ardagh'. The line's vocabulary — internal spaciousness, feelings happening within you rather than to you — fits his teaching register, but I cannot place it in a specific book, course, or talk. Attribution plausible on style alone; spelling correction is the confident part of this verdict.

'Arland Gilbert' appears in mid-20th-century American quotation compilations and inspirational calendars with no biographical trace I can recover — no book, no institutional affiliation, nothing that would let the attribution be checked. This is the classic profile of a compilation-only name, where the quotation and the attribution were introduced together and copied ever since. I cannot verify the person or the line. Honest answer: unknown.

Consistently attributed to the English novelist and essayist Arnold Bennett (1867-1931), and the cadence — the balanced clauses, 'the cognition of the brain' set against 'the experience of the soul' — is a good match for his Edwardian self-improvement essays such as The Human Machine and Literary Taste (both 1908/1909). I cannot confirm which work it comes from, and I will not guess between them. Attribution is stable in the compilation record but unverified against Bennett's text.

The surname is misspelled: this is Arnold H. Glasow (1905-1998), the American humorist whose one-line aphorisms were syndicated for decades in Reader's Digest, Forbes, and Wall Street Journal fillers. 'Glascow' is a common corruption. The line is consistently credited to him and fits his epigram output exactly, but Glasow's work was published as scattered fillers rather than collected volumes, so pinning a first appearance is effectively impossible without archive access. Attribution likely correct, source unlocatable.

Arnold M. Patent is a real author — You Can Have It All (1984) and other books on universal principles — and the phrasing about belonging to the universe is idiomatic for his material. I cannot confirm the sentence in any specific title, and much of his teaching circulated through workshops and newsletters, which makes tracing harder. Plausible but unverified.

Widely attributed to Art Buchwald, often to a commencement address, but this is an aphorism with a longer anonymous history than the Buchwald credit suggests — the pun circulated in newspaper filler and advertising copy before it settled on him, and it has also been credited to others. Buchwald may well have used it; using a saying is not authoring it. Given the pattern of a floating one-liner attaching to a famous humorist, I would not treat the Buchwald credit as established. Genuine origin unknown to me.

results.earliest_print_source: The Hound of the Baskervilles, Arthur Conan Doyle, 1902 (serialized in The Strand Magazine, 1901-1902)
results.notes: Spoken by Sherlock Holmes early in The Hound of the Baskervilles (ch. 3, 'The Problem'), during the discussion of Dr. Mortimer's account. Standard caveat that the line is a character's, not the author speaking in his own voice, but Doyle is the correct author credit.

results.earliest_print_source: Parerga und Paralipomena, Vol. II, Arthur Schopenhauer, 1851; English in 'Further Psychological Observations,' Studies in Pessimism, trans. T. Bailey Saunders, 1890
results.notes: Genuine Schopenhauer, from the psychological observations in Parerga and Paralipomena vol. II. The familiar English wording is T. Bailey Saunders' translation, widely reprinted in the Studies in Pessimism selection. I am confident of the work but not of a page number.

A well-documented misattribution. No such passage exists in Schopenhauer's works; Wikiquote carries it in the misattributed/disputed section. What Schopenhauer actually wrote (preface to the second edition of The World as Will and Representation, 1844) is the different and less tidy observation that truth is allowed only a brief celebration of victory between the long period in which it is condemned as paradoxical and the long period in which it is disparaged as trivial. The 'three stages' formula circulated in the 20th century with no source; a structurally similar three-stage remark about scientific truth is attributed to Louis Agassiz in the 19th century. I cannot identify the actual originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution.

Asha Tyson is an American motivational author (best known for 'How I Retired at 26!'). This passage circulates very widely on inspirational sites with her name attached and I have no reason to doubt it, but I cannot place it in any specific book, article, or talk from training knowledge, and the attribution appears to rest entirely on quote-aggregator repetition. Honest verdict: plausible author, no traceable source.

results.earliest_print_source: In One Era and Out the Other, Sam Levenson, 1973 ('Time Tested Beauty Tips')
results.notes: Not written by Audrey Hepburn. The first portion ('For attractive lips... helping hand at the end of each of your arms') is Sam Levenson's poem 'Time Tested Beauty Tips,' written for his newborn grandchild and published in his 1973 book. Hepburn reportedly read it aloud to her sons at Christmas near the end of her life, which is how her name became attached; her son Sean Hepburn Ferrer has publicly credited Levenson. The later sentences here ('The beauty of a woman is not in the clothes she wears...') are a separate accretion from anonymous chain-letter circulation and are not Levenson's either. This text is a composite, and the Hepburn credit is wrong.

Ayya Khema (1923-1997), the German-born Theravada nun who wrote 'Being Nobody, Going Nowhere,' is a plausible author: the vocabulary (wholesome/unwholesome, mindfulness as a state rather than a discourse) matches her teaching idiom closely. But I cannot place this passage in a specific book or dhamma talk, and much of her published material is transcribed talks, which makes exact sourcing hard. Attribution is credible but unverified.

Consistently attributed to Babe Ruth across sports-quote collections, but I know of no primary source: no interview, autobiography passage, or contemporary newspaper citation I can name. Ruth is a moderate misattribution magnet for aphorisms about teamwork and perseverance. Plausible but unsourced.

The formula long predates Banksy. Its ancestor is Finley Peter Dunne's 1902 Mr. Dooley line about the newspaper that 'comforts th' afflicted, and afflicts th' comfortable,' which was subsequently applied to journalism generally and then adapted to art. The art-specific phrasing is most often credited to the artist and educator Cesar A. Cruz. Banksy is a magnet for unsourced art aphorisms and I know of no place in 'Wall and Piece' or in his documented statements where he claims this line. Reattribution offered with the caveat that the Cruz credit is itself weakly sourced.
results.suggested_reattribution: Cesar A. Cruz (art phrasing); formula ultimately from Finley Peter Dunne, 1902

results.notes: Barbara Rose is a contemporary self-help/spirituality author ('Individual Power,' 'If God Was Like Man'). The passage matches her register, and the attribution is consistent across the inspirational-quote ecosystem, but I cannot locate it in a specific title from training knowledge. Note also the name collision with Barbara Rose the art historian, which makes aggregator attributions less reliable than they look.

Same situation as the other Barbara Rose entry in this batch: register and attribution are consistent with her published self-help writing, and the exercise-style prompts suggest a book or newsletter with a workbook element, but I cannot name the source. No independent evidence beyond quote-site repetition.

Barbara Sher is very likely the real author; this is one of her signature ideas and the phrasing matches her voice. My recollection points to 'Wishcraft: How to Get What You Really Want' (1979, with Annie Gottlieb) as the probable source, but I cannot confirm that with enough certainty to record it as a citation, so I am leaving the print-source field null rather than guessing. Attribution credible, source unconfirmed.

Barry Brailsford is a New Zealand author and storyteller associated with Waitaha and Maori traditions ('Song of Waitaha,' 'Wisdom of the Four Winds'). The content is consistent with his body of work, but I cannot place the passage in a specific book. Worth flagging separately that Brailsford's Waitaha material is itself contested by some Maori scholars regarding its provenance as traditional knowledge, which is a sourcing concern beyond the quote attribution.

Two problems. First, the author name is misspelled: the person usually credited is Barry LePatner, a New York construction attorney. Second, and more important, the aphorism substantially predates him. Versions of 'good judgment comes from experience, and experience comes from bad judgment' circulated in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and have been variously attributed to Will Rogers, Mark Twain, Rita Mae Brown, Jim Horning, and an anonymous cowboy or Persian proverb. It is a floating saying with no established originator; the LePatner credit appears to be a modern quote-book convention. I cannot name the true source, so no reattribution is offered.

I cannot identify this Ben Irwin or place this line in any published work. The name is common enough (a contemporary author writing on faith, among others) that the attribution cannot be pinned to a specific person with confidence. The line reads like an anonymous aphorism that acquired a name in circulation. Honest answer: unknown.

No source in Franklin's writings, letters, or almanacs. The internal evidence argues against him outright: the right to pursue happiness appears in the Declaration of Independence, not the Constitution, and Franklin, a signer of both, would be an unlikely person to confuse them. The line reads as a 20th-century American aphorism retrofitted onto Franklin, who is one of the heaviest misattribution magnets in the corpus alongside Twain and Lincoln. I cannot identify an actual originator, hence apocryphal rather than a reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: Poor Richard's Almanack, Benjamin Franklin, 1746; reprinted in 'The Way to Wealth,' 1758
results.notes: Genuine Franklin. The correct wording is 'Dost thou love life? Then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made of' — the input's 'Does thou' is a transcription error and should be corrected to 'Dost thou' before the quote goes live. First published in Poor Richard's Almanack and later gathered into the preface essay 'The Way to Wealth' (1758).

Bennett W. Goodspeed was an investment writer best known for 'The Tao Jones Averages: A Guide to Whole-Brained Investing' (1983), a book built around exactly this kind of right-brain/left-brain aphorism, and my recollection associates the line with him. I cannot confirm the book or page with enough certainty to record a citation, so the print-source field stays null. Attribution plausible, source unconfirmed.

Bernie Siegel, the surgeon and author of 'Love, Medicine and Miracles' (1986) and 'Peace, Love and Healing,' is a plausible author and the sentiment is squarely within his body of work. I cannot place the passage in a specific book, and Siegel's material is heavily excerpted in devotional anthologies without citation, which is how unsourced attributions to him propagate. Credible but unverified.

The idea is genuinely Russell's but this exact wording is not sourced. The documented original is from his 1933 essay 'The Triumph of Stupidity': 'The fundamental cause of the trouble is that in the modern world the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt.' Several loose paraphrases circulate, including the popular 'the whole problem with the world is that fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves, and wiser people so full of doubts,' which Wikiquote carries as unsourced. The text here ('the biggest cause of trouble... stupid people... intelligent folks') is another such variant, with an American register that does not sound like Russell. Recommend replacing with the sourced 1933 wording if this quote is wanted in the corpus.

Betty Eadie is the author of 'Embraced by the Light' (1992) and 'The Awakening Heart.' The passage's shift into second-person reflective prompts mid-paragraph suggests a devotional or workbook context rather than her narrative memoir, and it may be a compiler's stitching of separate lines. I cannot place it in a specific title. Also note the stray closing double-quote at the end of the text, which should be cleaned before publication.

The Betty Reese credit is the conventional one in quote books from roughly the 1980s onward, where she is usually identified only as an American public relations executive — an unusually thin biographical trail for an attribution. The mosquito image belongs to a larger family of sayings, including the widely circulated 'if you think you are too small to make a difference, try sleeping with a mosquito,' which is variously credited to the Dalai Lama and to an African proverb, none of them with a solid primary source. Attribution exists but is weak.

Consistently and long attributed to Bill Cosby, who is generally reported to have said it in interviews; the attribution is stable and I am not aware of any competing claimant or earlier appearance, which is why this sits above the pure-unverified tier. But I cannot name the interview, book, or date, so it falls short of the 0.80 promotion bar. Separate from provenance, the corpus owner may want to consider whether Cosby attributions belong in an inspirational collection at all.

Ubiquitous in leadership training material and consistently credited to Gates, usually with a vague pointer to a late-1990s speech, but I cannot name the occasion or a printed text. The 'next century' framing places the origin plausibly in the 1990s, which is consistent with the attribution without confirming it. Widely repeated is not the same as sourced.

results.earliest_print_source: Lady Sings the Blues, Billie Holiday with William Dufty, 1956 (as commonly cited; I cannot confirm the page)
results.notes: My recollection places this line in Holiday's autobiography 'Lady Sings the Blues,' and the imagery — white satin, gardenias, the plantation — is characteristic of that book's account of touring as a Black singer with white bands. Two caveats keep it below the promotion bar: I cannot confirm the page or chapter, and the book was ghostwritten by William Dufty, with scholars (notably Farah Jasmine Griffin and John Szwed) documenting that substantial parts of it are unreliable or not in Holiday's own words. The sentiment is authentically hers; the exact authorship of the sentence is shared with Dufty.

The circle teaching is authentically Black Elk's, but this terse six-word phrasing does not match the known texts. The famous passage in 'Black Elk Speaks' (John G. Neihardt, 1932) runs 'Everything the Power of the World does is done in a circle,' continuing through the round sky, the round sun and moon, and the whirling wind; 'The Sacred Pipe' (Joseph Epes Brown, 1953) develops the same idea. 'Everything sacred moves in a Circle' appears to be a condensation that circulates without a source. Additional caveat: both books are non-Lakota interlocutors' renderings of Black Elk's words, so even the canonical wordings are mediated. Recommend replacing with the sourced Neihardt line if this idea is wanted.

results.earliest_print_source: Pensées, Blaise Pascal, 1670 (fragment 139 Brunschvicg / 136 Lafuma)
results.notes: Genuine Pascal. French original: 'tout le malheur des hommes vient d'une seule chose, qui est de ne savoir pas demeurer en repos dans une chambre.' The English wording here is one of several standard translations ('All of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone' is the other common rendering). Attribution is not in doubt; only the translation varies.

Consistent with Brian Greene's voice and subject matter, and I recall it circulating from 'The Elegant Universe' (1999), in the discussion of how relativity forces us to give up intuitions about space and time. I cannot place the chapter or page with enough certainty to cite it, so the print source is left null rather than guessed. No competing attribution exists, which supports the author even without a located source.

Brian Tracy is a real motivational author whose seminars and books (e.g. 'Maximum Achievement', 'Goals!') repeat this theme, and the attribution is consistent across quote aggregators. But the passage reads like transcribed seminar speech and I cannot place it in a specific book, article, or recorded talk. Plausible but unsourced; no competing attribution.

Widely and consistently attributed to Brian Tracy across quote collections and his own promotional material, with no rival claimant I know of. However the maxim belongs to a large family of older success-literature sayings about 'going the extra mile' (Napoleon Hill and Elbert Hubbard both worked this ground), so an earlier ancestor is possible. No specific book or talk locatable.

The line is much older than Brian Tracy. The known original is Elizabeth Bibesco (1897-1945, daughter of H. H. Asquith): 'Blessed are those who can give without remembering and take without forgetting.' It appears in her posthumous collection 'Haven' (1951) and is standardly attributed to her. Tracy and other motivational speakers quote it, which is how his name became attached. I am confident about Bibesco as the source of the saying but am not citing a page, so the print field is null.

I cannot place this in any authenticated Bruce Lee material ('Tao of Jeet Kune Do', 'Striking Thoughts', 'Artist of Life', or the interview record). It reads as a reworded version of the well-known aphorism 'Change is inevitable; growth is optional,' which is generally attributed to John C. Maxwell. Because the wording here differs materially and I cannot confirm the derivation chain, I am not asserting a reattribution. Bruce Lee is a moderate misattribution magnet: his notebooks copied maxims from mid-century self-help writers, and quote sites then credit him for them.

Genuinely Bruce Lee in substance. The 'be like water' teaching is documented on film in two 1971 sources: the Pierre Berton Show interview (December 1971) and the Longstreet episode 'The Way of the Intercepting Fist,' which carries the famous 'Be water, my friend.' The exact sentence quoted here appears to be a compressed/merged rendering of that spoken material rather than a verbatim line from a single source, so I am withholding a specific citation. Author attribution is safe; wording is approximate.

This is Wendell Phillips, the American abolitionist orator: 'What is defeat? Nothing but education, nothing but the first step to something better.' It is a well-established Phillips line from his mid-19th-century speeches and appears in standard quotation dictionaries under his name. Bruce Lee transcribed passages from other writers into his personal notebooks, and posthumous compilations plus quote sites have credited several such borrowings to him. Confident in Phillips as the originator.

Circulates under Bruce Lee's name but I cannot place it in his authenticated writings, and the phrasing is pure mid-century American positive-thinking literature (Napoleon Hill / Norman Vincent Peale register). Lee read and copied from those authors, so this may be another borrowed maxim recorded in his notebooks. I do not have a specific prior source, so no reattribution is asserted.

Among the better-supported Bruce Lee lines. I recall it from his own written notes as collected in the John Little-edited volumes, most likely 'Striking Thoughts: Bruce Lee's Wisdom for Daily Living' (2000). I am confident enough in Lee's authorship to call it attributed, but not confident enough about the exact volume and page to enter a print citation, so that field is null.

The widely circulated form is 'The successful warrior is the average man, with laser-like focus'; this entry is a de-gendered variant of that. I cannot locate either form in Bruce Lee's authenticated writings or interviews, and 'laser-like focus' is a late-20th-century business-motivation idiom rather than Lee's vocabulary. Probably a modern coinage that acquired his name. No alternative originator known.

Bruno Gröning (1906-1959) was a German faith healer, and this sentiment matches the teaching material published by the Bruno Gröning Circle of Friends, which is essentially the only body that transmits his sayings. That transmission is devotional and post-hoc rather than documentary, and I know of no contemporaneous published text or recording I could point to for this line. The attribution is plausible within that tradition but unverifiable from what I know.

Authentic Fuller vocabulary and syntax; in his own usage the subject is 'the comprehensive designer,' described as an emerging synthesis of artist, inventor, mechanic, objective economist and evolutionary strategist. My recall places it in 'Ideas and Integrities: A Spontaneous Autobiographical Disclosure' (1963), where the comprehensive designer is his central figure, but I am not certain enough to enter that as the citation. Author attribution is solid; the quoted version has been trimmed from 'comprehensive designer' to 'designer.'

results.earliest_print_source: Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth, R. Buckminster Fuller, 1969
results.notes: Core Fuller, and the 'Spaceship Earth' framing plus the closing 'It has to be everybody or nobody' are both signature formulations of his from this period. I place the passage in 'Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth' (1969); Fuller also repeated the 'everybody or nobody' line in later lectures and in 'Critical Path' (1981), so the exact wording here may reflect one of those restatements rather than the 1969 text verbatim.

results.earliest_print_source: I Seem To Be A Verb, R. Buckminster Fuller, 1970
results.notes: This is Fuller's best-known self-description and it gave the 1970 book its title. The passage is reproduced widely from that source and is not contested. Confidence held at 0.85 rather than higher only because Fuller recycled the formulation across talks and books and I cannot confirm which appearance is earliest.

Not canonical Buddhism. This is a member of the 'watch your thoughts, they become words' family of sayings, which has been variously credited to the Buddha, Lao Tzu, Gandhi, and Margaret Thatcher, and whose traceable modern ancestors are the 'sow a thought, reap an act; sow an act, reap a habit; sow a habit, reap a character; sow a character, reap a destiny' formula (attributed in the 19th century to Charles Reade and to Samuel Smiles) and a 1977 newspaper version credited to Frank Outlaw. None of these is Buddhist. I cannot identify which specific link in that chain produced this wording, so no reattribution is asserted.

results.earliest_print_source: The Dhammapada: The Sayings of the Buddha, trans. Thomas Byrom, 1976 (verses 1-2)
results.notes: This is Dhammapada 1-2 (Yamakavagga) in Thomas Byrom's 1976 rendering, which is the source of the familiar 'We are what we think' opening. Byrom is a free poetic translator: more literal versions render the opening as 'Mind precedes all mental states; mind is their chief.' So the underlying text is canonical and the ox-cart and shadow similes are genuine, but the English is Byrom's interpretation rather than a close translation. Attribution to 'Buddha' is correct in the traditional sense.

Not canonical. My recall places this in Jack Kornfield's 'Buddha's Little Instruction Book' (1994), a collection of Kornfield's own modern distillations written in the Buddha's voice, which is the documented origin of a whole cluster of pseudo-Buddha quotes now in circulation. The generic label 'Buddhist saying' is not false in spirit, but the line is a contemporary Western teacher's composition rather than a traditional saying. Reattribution offered with moderate rather than high confidence.

The input's own label is the honest one: this is a paraphrase, not a translation. The Kalama Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 3.65) is genuine canon and does urge the Kalamas not to accept teachings merely on the grounds of report, tradition, hearsay, scripture, logic, or a teacher's authority. But this English wording is a loose 19th/20th-century Western rendering of unknown authorship, and its final clause ('believe only what you yourself judge to be true') distorts the sutta, which asks the listener to test claims against whether they lead to harm or benefit and to weigh the judgment of the wise, not to make private judgment the sole criterion. Canonical basis real; this specific text unsourced and tendentious.

I can find no canonical or traditional Buddhist basis for this in what I know, and the aphorism's shape - an epigram about exploration and rarity - belongs to modern inspirational writing rather than to Pali or Mahayana sources. Origin unknown; the 'Buddhist saying' label appears to be decorative.

There is a genuine Buddhist antecedent for the candle image: the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters uses the simile of a torch from which many torches are lit without the original's light being diminished, applied to rejoicing in another's giving. So the first sentence has real textual ancestry. The second sentence, 'Happiness never decreases by being shared,' is a modern English addition, and the combined form circulating under the Buddha's name is not a translation of any single canonical passage. Genuine root, modern composite wording.

Doctrinally unobjectionable - samadhi as the proximate cause of panna is standard Theravada teaching, and Dhammapada 282 says meditation gives rise to wisdom - but I cannot match this seven-word sentence to any canonical verse or standard translation. It reads as a modern summary of the threefold training rather than a quotation. Sentiment traditional, wording unsourced.

This is a recognisable paraphrase of Udana 8.3 (the Nibbana Sutta): 'There is, monks, an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned. If there were not, there would be no escape from the born, become, made, conditioned.' The canonical source is secure, so the Buddhist attribution is sound, but the sentence as quoted matches no standard translation I know - it converts the sutta's existence claim into a claim about seeing and being liberated.
